sections.title: What Is Terraform?
paragraphs: Terraform is an open-source Infrastructure as Code (IaC) tool created by HashiCorp. It lets you describe your entire cloud environment, servers, networks, databases, DNS records, load balancers, in plain text configuration files, and then creates, updates, or destroys that infrastructure automatically.
Instead of clicking through the AWS Console to launch an EC2 instance, you write a few lines of configuration like this:
Run one command (terraform apply) and the server exists. Run another (terraform destroy) and it is gone. No clicks, no forgotten settings, no "I wonder what I configured last time."

sections.title: What Is Infrastructure as Code?
paragraphs: Infrastructure as Code (IaC) means treating your infrastructure the same way developers treat application code: write it in files, store it in Git, review it in pull requests, and deploy it automatically.

Before IaC, teams managed infrastructure manually. A senior engineer would click through the cloud console, configure something, and the knowledge of how it was configured lived only in their head, or a messy wiki page nobody kept up to date.

sections.title: Frequently Asked Questions
paragraphs: What is Terraform used for?

Terraform provisions and manages infrastructure by describing it in configuration files rather than clicking through a console. You declare the resources you want, networks, servers, databases, DNS records, and Terraform works out what to create, change or destroy to make reality match. Because the configuration lives in version control, infrastructure changes get reviewed, diffed and rolled back the same way application code does, and an identical environment can be recreated on demand.
What is the difference between Terraform and Ansible?

Terraform is a provisioning tool: it creates and destroys infrastructure and tracks what exists in state. Ansible is a configuration management tool: it installs packages and configures software on machines that already exist. Terraform is declarative and works out the changes needed to reach your desired state; Ansible is primarily procedural, running tasks in order. They are complementary rather than competing, and a common pattern is Terraform to build the servers and Ansible to configure what runs on them.
Should I use Terraform or CloudFormation?

Terraform if you use more than one provider or want the skill to transfer between employers. It works across AWS, Azure, GCP, Kubernetes, Datadog, Cloudflare and hundreds of others with one language and one workflow. CloudFormation is AWS-only but needs no state file of your own, since AWS manages it, and StackSets deploy across an entire AWS Organization with no open-source Terraform equivalent. Many AWS teams run both: CloudFormation or CDK for account baselines, Terraform for application infrastructure.
Is Terraform still open source?

Terraform moved from the Mozilla Public License to the Business Source License in 2023, which restricts using it to build a competing commercial product but leaves normal infrastructure use unaffected. In response the community forked the last MPL version as OpenTofu, now under the Linux Foundation and largely a drop-in replacement. For most teams either works and the configuration language is the same; the choice comes down to licensing preference and which ecosystem your tooling targets.
Do I need to know a cloud provider before learning Terraform?

Yes, at least the basics of one. Terraform is a way to express infrastructure, not a substitute for understanding it. A aws_vpc resource still requires you to know what a VPC, a subnet and a route table are, and error messages come from the provider rather than from Terraform. Learn the fundamentals of one cloud first, then Terraform becomes a much faster way to work with what you already understand.
What is the hardest part of Terraform for beginners?

State. Terraform records what it created in a state file, and almost every confusing situation. A resource it wants to recreate for no obvious reason, a change made in the console that Terraform undoes, two people applying at once and corrupting the file. Traces back to state. Set up a remote backend with locking before working in a team rather than after, and spend time understanding what state is for early; it pays back more than any other Terraform concept.

sections.title: Installing on macOS

To upgrade to a newer version later:
If you do not use Homebrew, download the binary directly:

# Add the official HashiCorp tap

sections.title: Installing on Linux
paragraphs: Add the official HashiCorp repository and install:
To upgrade later, run sudo apt-get update && sudo apt-get upgrade terraform.
Tip: Replace linux_amd64 with linux_arm64 if you are on an ARM machine such as a Raspberry Pi or AWS Graviton instance.

codeBlock.code:
# Install dependencies
sudo apt-get update && sudo apt-get install -y gnupg software-properties-common

# Add HashiCorp's GPG key
wget -O- https://apt.releases.hashicorp.com/gpg | \
  sudo gpg --dearmor -o /usr/share/keyrings/hashicorp-archive-keyring.gpg

# Add the repository
echo "deb [signed-by=/usr/share/keyrings/hashicorp-archive-keyring.gpg] \
  https://apt.releases.hashicorp.com $(lsb_release -cs) main" | \
  sudo tee /etc/apt/sources.list.d/hashicorp.list

# Install Terraform
sudo apt-get update && sudo apt-get install terraform

sections.title: Frequently Asked Questions
paragraphs: How do I install Terraform?

Use your platform's package manager: brew install terraform on macOS after adding the HashiCorp tap, the official apt or yum repository on Linux, or winget install HashiCorp.Terraform on Windows. Terraform is a single static binary, so downloading the release archive and putting the binary on your PATH works anywhere. Confirm with terraform version, which also warns you when a newer release is available.
How do I manage multiple Terraform versions?

Use tfenv, which installs and switches between versions per project. Create a .terraform-version file in the repository and tfenv selects the matching version automatically, so everyone on the team and your CI pipeline run the same one. This matters because Terraform writes a version marker into state, and a newer version will upgrade the state format. After which older versions can no longer read it. Pinning avoids one person accidentally upgrading state for everybody.
What should go in .gitignore for a Terraform project?

At minimum .terraform/ (downloaded providers and modules, which are large and machine-specific), *.tfstate and *.tfstate.backup (state belongs in a remote backend, and contains secrets in plain text), crash.log, and any *.tfvars files holding real values. Do commit .terraform.lock.hcl, which pins provider versions and makes builds reproducible. It is frequently gitignored by mistake, which defeats its purpose entirely.
Should I commit the .terraform.lock.hcl file?

Yes. It records the exact provider versions and their checksums, so everyone on the team and your CI pipeline resolve identical providers rather than picking up a new minor release independently. It is the direct equivalent of a package-lock.json or Cargo.lock. Update it deliberately with terraform init -upgrade when you intend to move provider versions, and review the resulting diff like any other dependency change.
How should I structure a Terraform project?

For anything small, a single directory with main.tf, variables.tf, outputs.tf and versions.tf is perfectly adequate. Splitting by resource type too early adds navigation cost with no benefit. As it grows, separate by environment with shared modules rather than copying configuration, so environments/production and environments/staging both call the same module with different values. Keep each environment's state separate, which prevents a staging mistake from touching production.
Do I need OpenTofu instead of Terraform?

Only if the Business Source License is a problem for you. OpenTofu is a fork of the last MPL-licensed Terraform, now under the Linux Foundation, and is close to a drop-in replacement with the same configuration language and workflow. For ordinary infrastructure work either is fine. Check which your team's tooling, modules and CI integrations target, since a few vendor integrations still assume one or the other.

sections.title: Introduction & Overview
paragraphs: Understand the Terraform init, plan, apply and destroy loop: what each command does, how to read a plan and the mistakes that cause outages.

Every Terraform project, from a single S3 bucket to a multi-account platform, runs the same four-command loop. Learning what each command actually does, rather than treating them as magic words, is what makes the rest of Terraform predictable.

sections.title: The four commands
paragraphs: The loop is write → init → plan → apply, repeated for the life of the project. destroy sits outside it and is used deliberately.

codeBlock.code:
terraform init      # once per project, and after provider/backend changes
terraform plan      # every time, before applying
terraform apply     # after reading the plan
terraform destroy   # when tearing an environment down

sections.title: What actually happens at each step
paragraphs: Downloads provider plugins into .terraform/, fetches external modules, configures where state lives, and writes .terraform.lock.hcl pinning exact provider versions.

Nothing else works until it has run, without providers loaded, Terraform does not know what an aws_instance is. Re-run it after adding a provider, changing a version constraint, adding a module, or changing the backend. Terraform tells you when it is needed.
Commit .terraform.lock.hcl; gitignore .terraform/.
This is the step that distinguishes Terraform from clicking in a console. It refreshes state against the real world, compares that to your configuration, and prints exactly what it would do.
Four symbols, and one of them matters far more than the others:

-/+ is the one to read every time. It means the attribute you changed cannot be modified in place, so Terraform will delete the resource and build a new one. On a stateless resource that is fine. On a database, a volume, or anything holding data, it is data loss arriving through what looked like a routine change. Terraform annotates the responsible attribute with # forces replacement, so the cause is always stated.
The summary line, 1 to add, 1 to change, 1 to destroy, is the fastest sanity check that you are pointed at the environment you think you are.
Builds a dependency graph, executes changes in order, runs independent resources in parallel, and writes state as it goes.

If it fails partway, Terraform does not roll back. Resources already created are kept and recorded, because destroying successfully created infrastructure is usually worse. Fix the cause and apply again. Terraform reconciles from where it is.
Removes every resource in state for that configuration and workspace. Preview it first with terraform plan -destroy, and protect anything important with lifecycle { prevent_destroy = true }.

sections.title: Two commands that belong in the loop
paragraphs: Neither touches infrastructure, and both belong in CI:
fmt ends formatting debates by having one right answer. validate catches typos, wrong argument names and type errors without contacting a provider, so it fails in seconds rather than at plan time.
Run fmt -check in CI so unformatted code cannot merge.

codeBlock.code:
terraform fmt -recursive    # canonical formatting
terraform validate          # syntax and internal consistency

sections.title: How the workflow changes in a team
paragraphs: Working alone, the loop above is enough. The moment a second person or a pipeline is involved, three things must change.
State moves to a remote backend with locking. Local state cannot be shared, has no version history, and two simultaneous applies will corrupt it. See Remote Backends.
Plan and apply become separate, reviewed steps. The pipeline plans on a pull request and posts the output for review, then applies on merge. Critically, it applies a saved plan file:
Without -out, the apply recalculates and may not match what was reviewed. With it, the approved change is the applied change.
Environments get separate state. Production and staging in one state file means one mistake reaches both.

codeBlock.code:
terraform plan -out=tfplan -input=false
# reviewed and approved
terraform apply tfplan

sections.title: The mistakes that cause real problems
paragraphs: Applying without reading the plan. Particularly missing a -/+ on something stateful.

Editing infrastructure in the console. Terraform will plan to undo it on the next run. If a change must be made by hand, bring it back into configuration promptly or Terraform becomes untrustworthy, and a tool people distrust gets bypassed, which compounds.
Committing state or .terraform/. State holds secrets in plain text; .terraform/ holds large binaries.
Using -target routinely. It is a recovery tool. Habitual use means part of your configuration is never validated against reality.
Not pinning provider versions. An unpinned provider can change behaviour between runs. Use required_providers with constraints and commit the lock file.

sections.title: Final Thoughts
paragraphs: The loop is four commands, but the discipline is one habit: read the plan before every apply. Almost every Terraform incident is a plan somebody scrolled past: a -/+ on a database, a destroy count larger than expected, or an apply against the wrong workspace. The plan tells you all three before anything happens.

sections.title: Frequently Asked Questions
paragraphs: What is the correct order of Terraform commands?

terraform init first, once per project and again whenever providers, modules or the backend change. Then terraform plan to see what would happen, and terraform apply to execute it. terraform destroy tears everything down when an environment is no longer needed. In practice you also run terraform fmt and terraform validate before planning, and both belong in CI so unformatted or invalid configuration cannot merge.
Do I need to run terraform plan before apply?

terraform apply produces a plan and asks for confirmation, so technically no. You should anyway, and in a team you must. The plan is the only place Terraform tells you that a change will replace a resource rather than update it, which on a database means data loss. In CI, run plan -out=tfplan and apply that file, which guarantees the change reviewed is the change applied.
What does the -/+ symbol mean in a Terraform plan?

Replace: Terraform will destroy the existing resource and create a new one, because the attribute you changed cannot be modified in place. The plan annotates the responsible attribute with # forces replacement. This is the single most important thing to look for, since on stateless resources it is harmless and on anything storing data it is destructive. Protect critical resources with lifecycle { prevent_destroy = true } so a replacement cannot be applied by accident.
What happens if terraform apply fails halfway through?

Terraform stops and keeps whatever it successfully created, recording it in state. There is no rollback, because destroying working infrastructure is usually worse than leaving it. Fix the underlying problem and run apply again; Terraform reconciles from the current state and creates only what is still missing. If the process was killed rather than erroring, a state lock may remain and need clearing with terraform force-unlock.
How often do I need to run terraform init?

Once when you start, and again after anything it configures changes. Adding or upgrading a provider, adding or changing a module source, or modifying the backend. You also need it after cloning a repository, since .terraform/ is not committed. Terraform detects when initialisation is stale and refuses to proceed with a clear message, so you rarely have to remember.
What is the difference between terraform fmt and terraform validate?

fmt rewrites files into canonical formatting, indentation and alignment, and changes nothing about behaviour. validate checks that the configuration is syntactically valid and internally consistent: correct argument names, sensible types, references that resolve. Neither contacts a provider or touches infrastructure, both run in under a second, and both belong in CI, with fmt -check failing the build on unformatted code.

paragraphs: terraform init is the very first command you run in any Terraform project. It prepares your working directory so that every other Terraform command (plan, apply, destroy) can work correctly.
Think of it like npm install or pip install, it sets up the dependencies your project needs before you can do anything else.

Running init on this configuration downloads both the AWS and Random providers into .terraform/providers/. This directory can be hundreds of megabytes, always add it to .gitignore.
If you have a backend block configured, init connects to it and migrates state if needed:
When switching from local state to a remote backend, init asks:
terraform init writes .terraform.lock.hcl, a file that pins the exact provider versions downloaded:

sections.title: Frequently Asked Questions
paragraphs: What does terraform init actually do?

Four things. It downloads the provider plugins your configuration requires into .terraform/, fetches any external modules, configures the backend where state will be stored, and writes or verifies .terraform.lock.hcl with the exact provider versions and checksums. Until it has run, no other Terraform command works, because Terraform has no providers loaded and does not know where state lives.
When do I need to re-run terraform init?

Whenever the things it sets up change: after adding or changing a provider or its version constraint, after adding or updating a module source, after changing the backend configuration, and after cloning a repository for the first time since .terraform/ is not committed. Terraform tells you when it is needed with an error saying the configuration has changed since initialisation. Running it again when it is not needed is harmless.
What is the difference between terraform init and terraform init -upgrade?

Plain init respects .terraform.lock.hcl and installs exactly the provider versions recorded there, which is what makes builds reproducible. -upgrade ignores the locked versions, resolves the newest releases allowed by your version constraints, and rewrites the lock file. Use -upgrade deliberately when you intend to move provider versions, then review the lock file diff like any other dependency bump, never as a reflex when something is failing.
Should I commit the .terraform directory?

No. It contains downloaded provider binaries which are large, platform-specific and reproducible from the lock file, so committing them bloats the repository for no benefit. Add .terraform/ to .gitignore. Do commit .terraform.lock.hcl though, that is the small text file recording which versions to install, and it is what makes everyone's init produce the same result.
How do I run terraform init in CI?

Run it at the start of every job, since CI workspaces start empty. Use -input=false so it never waits for interactive input, and -backend-config to supply backend settings from environment variables or secrets rather than committing them. Caching the .terraform directory between runs speeds things up noticeably on large provider sets, but key the cache on the lock file so a provider change invalidates it.
Why does init fail with a provider registry error?

Usually network access or a version constraint that cannot be satisfied. In a restricted network the registry may be unreachable, in which case a provider mirror or a network policy change is needed. If the error names a version, your constraints conflict. Perhaps a module requires a provider version your root configuration excludes. Read the constraint chain in the error, which names each source, and reconcile them in required_providers.

sections.title: What Is terraform plan?
paragraphs: terraform plan is the safety net of Terraform. Before making any infrastructure changes, it calculates exactly what would happen and shows you a precise diff, without actually doing anything.

Think of it as asking Terraform: "If I run apply right now, what changes will happen?" The answer is printed as an execution plan: a line-by-line breakdown of every resource that will be created, updated, replaced, or deleted.
Running plan is always safe. It has zero side effects. No API calls are made to create or destroy resources. You can run it as many times as you like.

sections.title: Frequently Asked Questions
paragraphs: What does terraform plan do?

It compares your configuration against the recorded state and the real infrastructure, then prints exactly what it would change without changing anything. Resources are marked + to create, ~ to update in place, - to destroy, and -/+ to replace. It is the review step that separates Terraform from clicking in a console, and it should be read before every apply. Particularly for the -/+ symbol, which means a resource will be destroyed and recreated.
What does the -/+ symbol mean and why is it dangerous?

It means replace: Terraform will destroy the existing resource and create a new one, because the property you changed cannot be modified in place. On a stateless resource that is harmless. On a database, an EBS volume or anything holding data, it is data loss delivered by an apparently routine change. Terraform states the reason with a "forces replacement" annotation next to the offending attribute. Read every plan for this before applying to anything stateful.
Why does terraform plan show changes when I have not changed anything?

Usually drift. Something was changed outside Terraform, in a console or by another tool, and Terraform intends to bring it back in line. It can also be a provider upgrade that computes a default differently, a value that genuinely changes on every run such as a timestamp, or a resource whose API returns attributes in a different order. Read which attribute is changing: drift from a console edit is obvious, whereas a perpetual diff on the same attribute every run usually means a provider quirk that needs ignore_changes.
What is a saved plan file and should I use one?

terraform plan -out=tfplan writes the plan to a file, and terraform apply tfplan applies exactly that plan without recalculating. This matters in CI and for anything reviewed by a human, because it guarantees what was approved is what gets applied, without it, the state or the real infrastructure could change between the plan and the apply. The caveat is that a saved plan contains sensitive values in plain text, so treat it as a secret and do not archive it carelessly.
Should I use -target?

Sparingly, and as a recovery tool rather than a habit. -target limits the plan to specific resources, which is genuinely useful when untangling a partially failed apply or working around a dependency problem. It is not a normal workflow: Terraform warns about it because operating on a subset means the rest of your configuration is not validated against reality, and it is easy to leave infrastructure in a state that does not match the code. If you reach for it routinely, the configuration probably wants splitting up.
How do I use terraform plan in a CI pipeline?

Run terraform plan -input=false -out=tfplan on pull requests and post the output as a comment so the change is reviewable, then apply the saved plan file on merge. Use -detailed-exitcode, which returns 0 for no changes, 2 for changes present and 1 for an error, that lets a pipeline distinguish "nothing to do" from "changes await approval" and act accordingly. Never let apply run automatically from a feature branch against shared infrastructure.

sections.title: Frequently Asked Questions
paragraphs: What happens during terraform apply?

Terraform builds a dependency graph from your configuration, calculates the changes, shows them for approval, then executes them. Creating, updating and destroying resources in dependency order, with independent resources handled in parallel. As each resource completes, its attributes are written to state. Once the apply finishes, state reflects what now exists and any declared outputs are available via terraform output.
Should I use terraform apply -auto-approve?

In CI, yes, but only when applying a saved plan file that a human reviewed: terraform apply tfplan needs no approval flag because the plan is already fixed. Using -auto-approve on a fresh plan means nobody saw what was about to happen, and it recalculates against whatever state exists at that moment. Interactively, type the confirmation. The pause before destroying something is worth the three seconds.
What happens if terraform apply fails halfway through?

Resources created before the failure are kept and recorded in state. Terraform does not roll back, because destroying successfully created infrastructure is usually worse than leaving it. Fix the cause and run apply again; Terraform reconciles from where it is, creating only what is still missing. The state file is written continuously during apply, so an interrupted run rarely loses track of what was made. If the process was killed hard, a stale lock may need clearing with terraform force-unlock.
How does Terraform decide what to do in parallel?

It builds a dependency graph from references between resources and walks it, running up to ten operations concurrently by default. Resources that reference each other are serialised; independent ones are not. -parallelism=n adjusts the limit, which is occasionally worth lowering when a provider's API rate limits start returning errors under load, and rarely worth raising.
How do I get values out after an apply?

Declare output blocks and read them with terraform output, or terraform output -json for machine-readable form that scripts can parse with jq. In CI this is how you pass a generated URL, an IP address or a database endpoint to a later job. Outputs marked sensitive = true are hidden in console output but still present in -json and in state, so they are not a security control, only a protection against shoulder-surfing and log leakage.
What should I do if an apply leaves a resource in a broken state?

Check whether Terraform knows about it. If the resource was created but the provider errored afterwards, it is usually in state and a subsequent apply will fix or replace it. If it was created and Terraform lost track, import it with terraform import rather than letting a second apply create a duplicate. If state contains something that no longer exists, terraform state rm removes the entry so Terraform stops trying to manage it. Always run a plan and read it before acting on any of these.

sections.title: Frequently Asked Questions
paragraphs: What does terraform destroy actually delete?

Every resource recorded in the state file for that workspace and configuration. It does not touch resources created outside Terraform, and it does not touch other workspaces or other state files. The destroy plan is shown for approval first, and reading it is worth the time. The count of resources is the quickest sanity check that you are pointed at the environment you think you are.
How do I preview a destroy without actually destroying?

terraform plan -destroy produces the destroy plan without executing it, and -out saves it for review. This is the safe way to answer "what would go away", particularly before tearing down anything shared. In CI, generating a destroy plan and posting it for approval is the equivalent of the normal plan-then-apply flow.
How do I protect resources from accidental destruction?

Add lifecycle { prevent_destroy = true } to anything holding data. Terraform then refuses any plan that would destroy it, including a full terraform destroy, and you must remove the flag deliberately to proceed. Combine that with provider-level protection, RDS deletion protection, S3 bucket versioning and MFA delete, so a mistake has to get past more than one gate. Note prevent_destroy cannot stop a destroy triggered by the resource being removed from configuration entirely.
Can I destroy just one resource?

Yes, with terraform destroy -target=aws_instance.example, but treat it as a recovery tool rather than routine practice. Targeting operates on a subset, so the rest of your configuration is not reconciled and dependent resources may be left referencing something gone. A cleaner approach for permanent removal is to delete the resource from the configuration and run a normal apply, which Terraform plans with full dependency awareness.
What is the difference between terraform destroy and deleting resources in the console?

terraform destroy removes the resources and clears them from state, leaving everything consistent. Deleting in the console removes the resources but leaves state believing they exist, so the next plan shows Terraform intending to recreate them, which is drift, and at best confusing, at worst a surprise recreation of something expensive. If resources were removed outside Terraform, use terraform state rm to bring state back in line.
Should terraform destroy ever run automatically in CI?

Only for genuinely ephemeral environments. A per-pull-request preview stack that is torn down on merge, or a nightly cleanup of a sandbox account. Even then, scope it tightly with a separate state file and credentials that cannot reach production, so an error in the pipeline cannot destroy the wrong thing. For anything long-lived, destruction should require a human.

paragraphs: See how data flows through Terraform: input variables, locals and outputs, where each belongs, how variable precedence works and how to handle secrets safely.
Three constructs move data through a Terraform configuration, and choosing the right one is most of what makes a configuration readable.

The rule of thumb: if someone deploying needs to choose it, make it a variable. If it is derived logic you want to name once, make it a local. If something outside needs to read it, make it an output.

sections.title: Input variables
paragraphs: A variable with no default is required. Terraform prompts for it interactively, which in CI means a hung pipeline unless -input=false is set.
Always write a description. It is what terraform-docs renders and what a colleague reads instead of your source.
string, number, bool, plus collections, list(string), map(string), set(string), and structural types:
Typing an object rather than accepting any turns a runtime failure deep inside a resource into a clear type error at plan time. optional() with a default keeps the interface small for simple callers.
validation blocks are underused and cheap. Rejecting a bad value at plan time with your own message beats a provider error three resources later that names nothing useful.

sections.title: Passing values in
paragraphs: Five mechanisms, evaluated lowest to highest precedence:
Precedence is per variable, so a tfvars file setting one value leaves everything else at its default.
For real projects, keep a tfvars file per environment in version control, as long as it holds no secrets. That makes the configuration reproducible and the values reviewable.

codeBlock.code:
terraform apply -var-file=production.tfvars
terraform apply -var="instance_count=5"
export TF_VAR_environment=staging

sections.title: Secrets
paragraphs: Mark the variable sensitive and supply the value from outside:
sensitive = true redacts the value from plan and apply output. That is all it does. The value is stored in plain text in state, so state encryption and access control remain the actual protection.
Better still, do not pass secrets in at all. Read them at plan time from a secret manager:
The value then never exists in a tfvars file, a CI variable, or anyone's shell history.

sections.title: Local values
paragraphs: Locals name internal logic. They cannot be set from outside, and they are computed once per run:
The common-tags pattern is the most valuable use: one place to change your tagging convention, applied everywhere.

Locals can be overused. A configuration where every literal is indirected through a local is harder to read, not easier. Reserve them for values used several times, expressions complex enough that a name helps, and anything you expect to change.

sections.title: Outputs
paragraphs: Outputs do two jobs. They surface values to humans after an apply, and, more importantly, they are the only way a module returns anything to its caller. A parent module cannot reach inside a child to read a resource attribute, so anything a caller might need must be an output.
Note that sensitive outputs appear unredacted in -json, so avoid printing the whole document into a CI log.

sections.title: Final Thoughts
paragraphs: Variables in, locals for internal logic, outputs out. Most unreadable Terraform comes from blurring those lines. Parameterising things that never vary, or computing in-line what should be a named local. Keep the required variable surface small, give everything a description, and remember that sensitive protects logs rather than state.

sections.title: Frequently Asked Questions
paragraphs: What is the difference between a variable, a local and an output in Terraform?

An input variable is supplied from outside the configuration, by a tfvars file, the command line, an environment variable, or a parent module, and is how the same code serves different environments. A local value is computed inside the configuration and cannot be overridden externally; it exists to name derived logic and avoid repetition. An output exposes a value outward, either for a human to read after apply or for a parent module to consume. Variables flow in, locals stay internal, outputs flow out.
What is the precedence order for Terraform variable values?

Lowest to highest: the default in the declaration, then TF_VAR_ environment variables, then terraform.tfvars, then *.auto.tfvars files alphabetically, then -var-file on the command line, and finally -var, which beats everything. Precedence applies per variable, so a tfvars file that sets one value leaves the others at their defaults. When a value is not what you expect, printing it through terraform console is the quickest way to find which layer supplied it.
How do I keep secrets out of my Terraform configuration?

Do not put them in tfvars files that are committed. Mark the variable sensitive = true so it is redacted from output, then supply the value through an environment variable or a CI secret, or better, read it at plan time from AWS Secrets Manager, SSM Parameter Store or Vault with a data source, so it never exists in a file at all. Remember sensitive only hides values from console output; they are stored in plain text in state, which is why state encryption and access control matter regardless.
Do I need a tfvars file for every environment?

It is the common and workable pattern: dev.tfvars, staging.tfvars, production.tfvars, selected with -var-file. Keep them in version control so environment differences are reviewable, and keep secrets out of them. The alternative, separate directories per environment, each with its own backend, gives stronger isolation because credentials and state can be scoped separately, and is worth the extra structure once production is involved.
When should I use a local instead of a variable?

When the value is internal logic rather than something a caller chooses. A name prefix built from other variables, a map of common tags, a computed CIDR. All locals. If a person deploying would reasonably want to set it differently, it is a variable. A frequent mistake is making everything a variable, which produces modules with twenty inputs where three would do and makes them unpleasant to use.
Why can't I read a value from inside a module without an output?

Because the module interface is deliberately a contract. A parent module can only see what a child explicitly exposes through output blocks, which is what lets a module change its internals without breaking callers. If you need a value from a module, add an output for it, and when writing a module, expose anything a caller might plausibly want, since adding an output later is easy but callers have no way to work around a missing one.

sections.title: Frequently Asked Questions
paragraphs: How do I pass values to Terraform variables?

Several ways, and they combine. A terraform.tfvars file is picked up automatically, as is any *.auto.tfvars. Pass a specific file with -var-file=production.tfvars, a single value with -var="region=eu-west-1", or set an environment variable named TF_VAR_region. For real projects, keep values in a per-environment tfvars file under version control, as long as it contains no secrets, since that makes the configuration reproducible and reviewable.
What is the order of precedence for Terraform variables?

From lowest to highest: the variable's default, then environment variables prefixed TF_VAR_, then terraform.tfvars, then *.auto.tfvars in alphabetical order, then -var-file on the command line, and finally -var, which wins over everything. Later sources override earlier ones on a per-variable basis, so a tfvars file setting one value leaves the rest at their defaults.
How do I handle secrets in Terraform variables?

Do not put them in tfvars files that get committed. Mark the variable sensitive = true so its value is redacted from plan and apply output, then supply it through an environment variable, a CI secret, or, best, a data source that reads it from AWS Secrets Manager, SSM Parameter Store or Vault at plan time. Be aware sensitive only hides values from console output: they are stored in plain text in the state file, which is why state needs encryption and restricted access regardless.
What is the difference between a variable and a local value?

A variable is an input from outside the configuration. Something a caller supplies, and which differs between environments. A local is a value computed inside the configuration from variables, resources or expressions, and it cannot be overridden from outside. The rule of thumb: if someone deploying needs to choose it, make it a variable; if it is derived logic you want to name once and reuse, make it a local.
How do variable validation blocks work?

A validation block inside a variable declaration runs a condition against the supplied value and fails with your error message if it does not hold. This catches bad input at plan time with a clear explanation, rather than producing a confusing provider error later. For example rejecting an environment name that is not one of dev, staging or prod, or an instance type outside an approved list. It is one of the cheapest ways to make a module pleasant for other people to use.
Should every value be a variable?

No. Over-parameterising is a common mistake that makes a module hard to use and hard to reason about, because a caller faces twenty decisions where three would do. Make something a variable when it genuinely differs between callers or environments; use a local for internal logic, and hardcode values that should not vary. A module with sensible defaults and a small required surface is far more usable than one exposing every attribute.

sections.title: Frequently Asked Questions
paragraphs: What is the difference between locals and variables in Terraform?

A variable is an input supplied from outside, by a tfvars file, the command line, or a calling module, and can differ per environment. A local is computed inside the configuration and cannot be overridden externally. Use a variable when the person deploying needs to choose the value; use a local when you want to name a derived value once and reuse it. Locals are evaluated after variables, so they can reference them.
When should I use a local instead of repeating an expression?

Whenever the same expression appears more than twice, or whenever naming it makes the configuration easier to read. A local such as name_prefix = "${var.project}-${var.environment}" used across twenty resources means one place to change the convention, and the intent is obvious at every use site. The common-tags pattern, a locals block merging standard tags with per-resource ones, is the single most useful application.
Can locals reference other locals?

Yes, as long as there is no circular reference. Terraform resolves them as a dependency graph, so a local can build on another declared above or below it in the file. Locals can also reference variables, data sources and resource attributes. What they cannot do is reference something that depends on them, which produces a cycle error naming the chain.
Are locals evaluated once or per resource?

Once per plan or apply, not per resource that references them. The value is computed and reused, so a local containing an expensive expression is not recalculated for each use. Note that a local referencing a resource attribute that is unknown until apply will itself be unknown at plan time, which is why a plan sometimes shows (known after apply) in a place you expected a concrete value.
Can I use locals to avoid repeating tags?

Yes, and it is the idiomatic pattern. Define a common_tags local containing your organisation's standard tags, then merge(local.common_tags, { Name = "..." }) on each resource to add specifics. Many providers also support default_tags at the provider level, which applies tags to every resource automatically. Combining the two gives you provider-wide defaults plus per-resource additions with no repetition.
Can I overuse locals?

Yes. A configuration where every value is indirected through a local becomes harder to follow than one with a few literals, because reading any resource means jumping to the locals block and back. Reserve them for values used in several places, for expressions complex enough that a name aids comprehension, and for anything you expect to change. A single-use local wrapping a simple literal usually costs more in navigation than it saves.

terraform output prints them all, terraform output name prints one, and terraform output -json produces machine-readable output for scripts to parse with jq. The -raw flag prints a single string value without quotes, which is what you want when interpolating into a shell command. Outputs are read from state, so they are available any time after apply without re-running anything.
What does marking an output sensitive actually do?

It redacts the value in terraform plan and terraform apply console output, showing (sensitive value) instead. That is all. The value is still stored in plain text in the state file, still returned by terraform output -json, and still visible to anyone who can read state. It protects against a secret appearing in a CI log or a screenshot. It is not encryption, and it is not an access control.
Why does my output show "known after apply" in the plan?

Because it depends on an attribute that does not exist until the resource is created: an auto-generated ID, an assigned IP address, an ARN. Terraform cannot know it at plan time, so it shows a placeholder. This is normal and requires no action. If an output you expected to be static shows this, it is referencing a resource attribute rather than a variable or literal.
How do I pass outputs between modules?

A child module declares an output, and the parent references it as module.<name>.<output>. That value can then be passed as an input to another module, which is how you wire a network module's subnet IDs into a compute module. For passing values between separate root configurations with separate state, use a terraform_remote_state data source, though many teams prefer writing the value to SSM Parameter Store and reading it back, which avoids coupling one configuration's state to another's.
Can I use outputs in CI/CD pipelines?

Yes, and it is the standard way to hand values to later steps. Run terraform output -json > outputs.json and parse it, or use -raw to capture a single value into a shell variable. Typical uses are passing a load balancer DNS name to a smoke test, an ECR repository URL to a build step, or a cluster name to a deployment job. Remember sensitive outputs appear unredacted in -json, so avoid printing the whole document into a log.

sections.title: Final Thoughts
paragraphs: State is not an implementation detail you can ignore. It is the thing Terraform reasons from, and understanding it converts most Terraform confusion into something obvious. sections.title: Frequently Asked Questions
paragraphs: What is Terraform state and why can't Terraform work without it?

State is Terraform's record of which real-world resources correspond to which configuration blocks. Nothing in your code or in the cloud provider records that aws_instance.web is i-0abc123. State does. Without it Terraform cannot distinguish creating a resource from updating one it made previously, so every apply would create duplicates. State also caches attributes so plans are fast, and records dependencies so destroys happen in the right order.
Is it safe to commit the Terraform state file to Git?

No. State stores resource attributes in plain text, including generated passwords, private keys and anything passed through a variable marked sensitive, that flag only affects console output. Committing it exposes secrets to everyone with repository access and to Git history permanently. It also does not solve the problems a backend solves, since Git provides no locking, so two people can still apply simultaneously. Use a remote backend with encryption and restricted access.
What is a Terraform backend?

The configuration that tells Terraform where to store state and how to lock it. The default is local, writing terraform.tfstate to the working directory. Remote backends such as S3, Azure Blob Storage, Google Cloud Storage or Terraform Cloud store it centrally so it can be shared, versioned and locked. Switching is a matter of adding a backend block and running terraform init, which offers to migrate the existing state.
Why does state locking matter?

Because two simultaneous applies writing to the same state file will corrupt it, leaving Terraform with an inaccurate record of your infrastructure, which is considerably harder to fix than the original problem. Locking makes the second run wait or fail instead. It becomes essential the moment more than one person or a CI pipeline can apply, and it is the main reason local state does not scale beyond one developer.
How do I separate state between dev, staging and production?

Give each environment its own state file, typically a different key in the same backend bucket. This means a mistake in one cannot corrupt another's state, environments can be applied independently, and credentials can be scoped per environment. Terraform workspaces offer a lighter alternative, but they share one backend and one set of credentials, which is why separate state files, and ideally separate directories, are preferred for production.
What should I do if terraform plan shows changes I did not make?

That is drift: someone changed the infrastructure outside Terraform, and the plan is proposing to bring it back in line with your configuration. Run terraform plan -refresh-only to review what changed without mixing it with configuration changes. Then decide whether to accept the manual change by updating your code, or let Terraform revert it. Leaving drift unresolved is how teams stop trusting Terraform, and a tool people distrust gets bypassed.

sections.title: What Is Terraform State?
paragraphs: Terraform state is the record Terraform keeps of the infrastructure it manages. Every time Terraform creates, updates, or destroys resources, it writes information about those resources into state.

That state is usually stored in a file named terraform.tfstate when you are using local state. The file is machine-readable JSON, but the important idea is not the file format. The important idea is that Terraform needs a reliable memory of what it manages.

Without state, Terraform would have a serious problem: it could read your configuration, but it would not know whether the resources described in that configuration already exist, whether it created them before, or how those resources map to real objects in AWS, Azure, GCP, or another provider.
State solves that problem.

State is Terraform's record of which real resources correspond to which configuration blocks. State also caches resource attributes so plans can be produced without querying every API on every run, and it tracks dependencies so destroys happen in the right order.
Is the Terraform state file sensitive?

Yes, treat it as a secret. State stores resource attributes in plain text, which includes database passwords, generated keys and anything passed through a variable marked sensitive, that flag only redacts console output, not state. Never commit it to version control, store it in an encrypted remote backend with restricted access, and audit who can read it. A state file is often the single most valuable artifact in an infrastructure repository.
What happens if I lose the state file?

Terraform loses all knowledge of what it manages, and the next apply will try to create everything again. Producing duplicates or failing on name conflicts. Recovery means either restoring from a backup, which is why remote backends with versioning matter, or importing every existing resource back into a fresh state with terraform import, which is slow and error-prone for anything non-trivial. Enable versioning on the state bucket before you need it.
What is drift and how does Terraform detect it?

Drift is when real infrastructure no longer matches state, usually because someone changed something in a console or another tool. Terraform detects it by refreshing, querying the provider for current attributes, and comparing against state during a plan, then showing the difference as changes it intends to make. That is why an untouched configuration can produce a non-empty plan: Terraform is proposing to undo the out-of-band change.
What is the difference between the .terraform directory and the state file?

.terraform/ is a local working directory holding downloaded provider binaries, fetched modules and backend configuration. It is disposable, machine-specific, recreated by terraform init, and belongs in .gitignore. The state file records what infrastructure exists and is irreplaceable. Losing .terraform costs you one init, while losing state can cost a rebuild of your entire environment.
Do I need remote state for a solo project?

Not strictly, but it is worth it early. Local state lives on one machine, so it is lost with that laptop, has no version history, and cannot be shared the moment a second person or a CI pipeline is involved. An S3 bucket with versioning and encryption takes ten minutes to set up and removes a whole category of future pain. Migrating later is possible but always less pleasant than starting that way.

paragraphs: Why do I need a remote backend?

Because local state cannot be shared, versioned or locked. A remote backend puts state somewhere every team member and your CI pipeline can reach, keeps it encrypted, and, critically, locks it so two people cannot apply at once and corrupt it. It also gives you version history, which is the difference between recovering from a bad state write in minutes and rebuilding an environment.
How do I set up an S3 backend with state locking?

Create an S3 bucket with versioning and encryption enabled, then point your backend "s3" block at it with a key naming the state path. Modern Terraform supports native S3 locking via use_lockfile, which removes the need for a separate DynamoDB table; older versions require a DynamoDB table with a LockID partition key referenced by dynamodb_table. Either way, the bucket and table must exist before terraform init. They cannot be created by the same configuration that stores its state in them.
How do I bootstrap the backend that stores my state?

The chicken-and-egg problem is real: the bucket must exist before Terraform can use it for state. Two workable approaches. Create the bucket and lock table in a small separate configuration with local state, committed alongside everything else. It changes rarely, so local state is tolerable. Or create the resources with a CLI script or CloudFormation once, then reference them. Some teams create the backend resources in Terraform with local state, then migrate that configuration's own state into the bucket it just made.
What happens if a state lock gets stuck?

Terraform refuses to proceed and reports the lock ID, who holds it and when it was acquired. This usually follows a process killed mid-apply. Confirm nobody is genuinely running an apply, then clear it with terraform force-unlock <LOCK_ID>. Do this carefully, force-unlocking while an apply is actually running is how state gets corrupted, which is exactly what locking exists to prevent.
Can I change the backend after I have started?

Yes. Update the backend block and run terraform init, and Terraform detects the change and offers to migrate the existing state to the new location. It copies rather than moves, so the old state remains as a fallback. Take a manual backup first regardless, and run a plan immediately afterwards expecting no changes. A non-empty plan after a backend migration means something did not transfer correctly.
How should I separate state between environments?

Use a separate state file per environment, typically by giving each its own key in the same bucket, production/terraform.tfstate, staging/terraform.tfstate. This means a mistake in staging cannot touch production state, blast radius is contained, and the two can be applied independently. Backend configuration cannot use variables, so supply the differing values with -backend-config at init time, or use separate directories per environment.

sections.title: Why Terraform State Commands Exist
paragraphs: Most of the time, Terraform updates state automatically. You run terraform plan and terraform apply, and Terraform handles the internal bookkeeping for you.

But real infrastructure projects are messy. Resource names change. Modules get reorganized. Existing cloud resources need to be brought under Terraform management. Sometimes you need to inspect state directly to understand what Terraform thinks it owns.
That is where Terraform state commands come in.
These commands let you inspect or carefully adjust Terraform's record of managed infrastructure without always changing the actual cloud resources themselves.
This is powerful, but it also means you must use these commands with care. Many of them affect Terraform's memory of infrastructure, not the infrastructure itself.

paragraphs: terraform import brings an existing real infrastructure object under Terraform management by associating it with a resource address in state.
This is crucial when resources already exist before Terraform is introduced.

sections.title: terraform refresh
paragraphs: Historically, terraform refresh updated state to reflect the current real infrastructure without changing resources.
Terraform queries the provider APIs, reads current infrastructure details, and updates the state accordingly.
This can help when you suspect drift or when you want Terraform's stored view to reflect the latest real-world information.

In modern Terraform workflows, many teams prefer terraform plan or terraform apply -refresh-only because they make refresh behavior more explicit and easier to review. But it is still important to understand the refresh concept because state must periodically be reconciled with reality.
Think of refresh as: update Terraform's state to match what exists right now.

sections.title: Frequently Asked Questions
paragraphs: When should I use terraform state commands?

Only when the normal plan-and-apply cycle cannot express what you need: renaming a resource in code without recreating it, moving resources into a module, removing something from Terraform's management without destroying it, or adopting existing infrastructure. They edit state directly and bypass the safety of a plan, so reach for them deliberately and take a state backup first. Every one of these has a way to make things worse.
How do I rename a resource without destroying it?

Rename it in the configuration, then run terraform state mv aws_instance.old aws_instance.new so state points the existing object at the new address. Without that, Terraform sees the old address gone and a new one added, and plans a destroy and create. Newer Terraform supports moved blocks in configuration, which express the same intent declaratively, are reviewable in a pull request, and are generally the better option.
What is the difference between terraform state rm and terraform destroy?

state rm removes the resource from Terraform's records but leaves the real infrastructure running. Terraform simply stops managing it. destroy deletes the actual resource. Use state rm when handing something over to another team or another configuration, or when Terraform is tracking something that no longer exists. Be careful: after state rm, a subsequent apply may try to create a fresh copy, since the configuration still declares it.
How do I import existing infrastructure into Terraform?

Write the resource block first, then run terraform import aws_instance.web i-0abc123 to bind it to the existing object. Import populates state but does not write configuration, so you must author the block yourself and run a plan afterwards to reconcile any differences. Expect several iterations until the plan is empty. Newer Terraform supports import blocks in configuration plus -generate-config-out, which drafts the resource block for you and makes adopting a large estate considerably less tedious.
Is terraform refresh still needed?

Rarely as a standalone command. terraform plan and terraform apply refresh state automatically before computing changes, so the separate command is largely redundant and is deprecated in favour of terraform apply -refresh-only, which shows what refreshing would change and asks for approval. That variant is genuinely useful for reviewing drift deliberately without applying any configuration changes alongside it.
How do I safely inspect what is in state?

terraform state list enumerates every managed resource address, and terraform state show <address> prints all recorded attributes for one. Both are read-only and safe to run at any time. They are the fastest way to answer "does Terraform know about this" and "what does Terraform think this resource looks like", which between them explain most confusing plans.

sections.title: Introduction & Overview
paragraphs: Learn what Terraform modules are, when to write one, how to design a clean interface, version and source them, and move resources in without recreating them.
A module is just a directory of .tf files. That is the whole definition, which means you have been writing modules since your first configuration, whether or not you called them that.
The directory you run Terraform in is the root module. Anything it calls with a module block is a child module.

sections.title: What modules are for
paragraphs: Without them, deploying the same pattern three times means copying sixty resources three times, and a fix has to be applied in three places. Where it inevitably gets applied in two.
A module packages those resources behind an interface of inputs and outputs:
That block creates a VPC, subnets across three zones, route tables, an internet gateway and NAT gateways, perhaps sixty resources, from twelve lines that state intent rather than mechanism.

codeBlock.code:
module "vpc" {
  source  = "terraform-aws-modules/vpc/aws"
  version = "~> 5.0"

  name = "production"
  cidr = "10.0.0.0/16"

  azs             = ["eu-west-1a", "eu-west-1b", "eu-west-1c"]
  private_subnets = ["10.0.1.0/24", "10.0.2.0/24", "10.0.3.0/24"]
  public_subnets  = ["10.0.101.0/24", "10.0.102.0/24", "10.0.103.0/24"]

  enable_nat_gateway = true
  single_nat_gateway = false
}

sections.title: When to create one
paragraphs: Not on the first use. Premature abstraction produces modules shaped around a single caller, with awkward inputs nobody else can use. Write the resources directly, write them a second time, notice the pattern, then extract.
Good signals that something should be a module:
Bad signals: wrapping a single resource in a module that adds nothing but indirection, or modularising because it feels tidier.

sections.title: Using someone else's
paragraphs: For well-trodden infrastructure, use the registry. The AWS VPC and EKS modules handle a large number of edge cases that take a long time to rediscover, and reimplementing either is rarely a good use of time.
Always pin version. A pessimistic constraint like ~> 5.0 allows patch and minor updates while preventing a major version arriving unannounced. For Git sources, pin a tag:
An unpinned module means an upstream change can alter your infrastructure the next time anyone runs init -upgrade.
Note the // in that Git source. It separates the repository from the subdirectory within it, which is how a monorepo of modules is referenced.

sections.title: Writing your own
paragraphs: Two design principles matter more than the rest.
Keep the required surface small. Everything that can have a sensible default should, so the simplest call is a few lines. A module with twenty required inputs is one people avoid.

Expose outputs generously. A caller cannot reach inside a module, so anything they might plausibly need, IDs, ARNs, endpoints, should be an output. Adding one later is easy; working around a missing one is not.

Do not declare a provider block inside a module. Declare required_providers in versions.tf to state what the module needs, and let the provider configuration be inherited from the root. A module with its own provider block cannot be used across regions or accounts, and cannot be removed cleanly from state.

codeBlock.code:
modules/s3-bucket/
├── main.tf        # resources
├── variables.tf   # inputs
├── outputs.tf     # outputs
├── versions.tf    # terraform and provider constraints
└── README.md      # usage example

sections.title: Moving resources into a module
paragraphs: This is where people get caught. Moving aws_instance.web into a module changes its state address to module.compute.aws_instance.web, so Terraform sees the old address gone and a new one appear, and plans a destroy and create.
Use a moved block, which declares the rename declaratively and is reviewable in a pull request:
Run a plan afterwards and confirm it is empty before applying. terraform state mv does the same thing imperatively and is fine for a one-off, but leaves no record in the codebase.

sections.title: How deep to nest
paragraphs: Shallowly. One or two levels is comfortable. Three or more makes debugging genuinely unpleasant, because tracing a value means walking several interfaces and errors arrive with long qualified addresses.
A workable structure is a root module per environment calling a handful of composed modules, each of which may call one layer of small building blocks. If you are counting levels, flatten it.

sections.title: Final Thoughts
paragraphs: Modules are how Terraform configurations stay maintainable past a few hundred lines, and how a pattern gets defined once instead of copied. The judgement is knowing when. Extract after the second repetition, not the first, and design the interface for the caller rather than for the implementation. Pin every version, keep nesting shallow, and use moved blocks when refactoring so a reorganisation never becomes a rebuild.

sections.title: Frequently Asked Questions
paragraphs: What is a Terraform module?

Any directory containing .tf files. The directory you run Terraform in is the root module; any directory it calls with a module block is a child module. Modules exist to package a group of related resources behind a defined interface of inputs and outputs, so a VPC with its subnets, route tables and gateways becomes one block with a few arguments rather than sixty resources repeated across projects.
When should I create a module instead of writing resources directly?

After the second repetition, not the first. Extracting too early produces modules shaped around one caller's needs, with awkward interfaces that do not generalise. Good signals are the same group of resources deployed more than twice, a set of resources with a coherent purpose worth naming, or several environments needing the same shape with different values. Wrapping a single resource in a module usually adds indirection without benefit.
Should I use community modules from the Terraform Registry?

For well-trodden infrastructure, yes. The AWS VPC and EKS modules in particular handle a large number of edge cases that are slow to rediscover. Write your own for patterns specific to your organisation, or when a community module's flexibility brings more complexity than your case justifies. A common middle path is wrapping a registry module in a thin internal one that fixes your naming and tagging conventions.
How do I pin a module version?

Set version with a pessimistic constraint such as ~> 5.0 when sourcing from a registry, which allows patch and minor updates but blocks an unannounced major version. For Git sources, use ?ref=v1.2.0 to pin a tag rather than tracking a branch. Without pinning, an upstream change can alter your infrastructure the next time anyone runs terraform init -upgrade, which is exactly the kind of surprise infrastructure code exists to prevent.
Why does Terraform want to recreate everything after I moved resources into a module?

Because the state address changed: aws_instance.web became module.compute.aws_instance.web, and Terraform treats the old address as removed and the new one as added. Add a moved block declaring the change, which is applied by a normal plan and is reviewable in a pull request, or use terraform state mv for a one-off. Either way, run a plan afterwards and confirm it is empty before applying.
Should a module contain its own provider block?

No. Declare required_providers in the module's versions.tf to state which providers and versions it needs, but leave the provider configuration, region, credentials, aliases, to the root module, which the child inherits. A module with its own provider block cannot be used with multiple regions or accounts and cannot be cleanly removed from state. When a module genuinely needs a non-default provider, pass an alias explicitly through the providers argument.

sections.title: What Are Terraform Modules?
paragraphs: A Terraform module is a directory that contains Terraform configuration files. That definition is surprisingly simple, but it is incredibly powerful.

Every Terraform working directory is already a module. The directory where you run terraform init, terraform plan, and terraform apply is called the root module. When the root module calls another module using a module block, that other module is called a child module.

Modules matter because they make infrastructure code reusable. Instead of copying the same VPC, subnets, security groups, and tags into many projects, you can define them once and reuse them with different inputs.

paragraphs: What is a Terraform module?

Any directory containing .tf files is a module. The directory you run Terraform in is the root module; anything it calls with a module block is a child module. Modules package a set of resources behind a defined interface of inputs and outputs, so a VPC with its subnets, route tables and gateways becomes one block with a few arguments rather than sixty resources copied between projects.
Should I use registry modules or write my own?

Use registry modules for well-trodden infrastructure where the edge cases are many and someone else has already handled them. The AWS VPC and EKS modules are the classic examples, and reimplementing either is rarely a good use of time. Write your own for patterns specific to your organisation, or when a registry module's flexibility brings more complexity than your use case justifies. Always set version when sourcing from a registry, ideally with a pessimistic constraint such as ~> 5.0 so patch updates flow but a major version cannot arrive unannounced. For Git sources, pin to a tag or commit SHA with ?ref=v1.2.0 rather than tracking a branch. An unpinned module means an upstream change can alter your infrastructure the next time anyone runs init -upgrade, which is exactly the surprise you want to avoid.
How do I pass values into and out of a module?

Inputs are arguments in the module block, matching the child's variable declarations. Outputs come back as module.<name>.<output> and are the only way to read anything from inside a module. You cannot reference a child's resources directly. This is deliberate: the interface is the contract, and it is what lets a module's internals change without breaking callers.
How deeply should I nest modules?

Shallowly. One or two levels is comfortable; three or more makes debugging painful, because tracing a value means walking through several interfaces and error messages arrive with long qualified addresses. A common and workable structure is a root module per environment calling a handful of composed modules, each of which may call one layer of small building-block modules. If you find yourself counting levels, flatten it.
Why does Terraform want to recreate resources after I move them into a module?

Because moving a resource into a module changes its state address from aws_instance.web to module.compute.aws_instance.web, and Terraform sees the old address gone and a new one appear. Fix it with moved blocks in configuration, which declare the rename and are reviewable in a pull request, or with terraform state mv for a one-off. sections.title: Frequently Asked Questions
paragraphs: When should I create a Terraform module?

When the same group of resources is deployed more than twice, or when a set of resources has a coherent purpose worth naming, "an application service" rather than a load balancer, target group, task definition and security group. Do not modularise on the first use: premature abstraction produces modules with awkward interfaces built around a single caller's needs. Write it twice, notice the pattern, then extract.
How should I design a module's interface?

Keep the required inputs small and give everything else a sensible default, so the simplest use is a few lines. Use variable validation blocks to reject bad input at plan time with a clear message rather than letting a provider error surface later. Expose outputs for anything a caller might plausibly need, IDs, ARNs, endpoints, since adding one later is easy but callers cannot reach inside. A good module is judged by how short its typical call site is.
What files should a module contain?

By convention main.tf for resources, variables.tf for inputs, outputs.tf for outputs, and versions.tf for Terraform and provider constraints. A README.md documenting inputs, outputs and a usage example matters more than people expect, since it is what a future colleague reads instead of the source. terraform-docs generates the input and output tables automatically from your declarations, which keeps documentation honest.
Should a module declare its own provider?

No. Modules should declare required_providers in versions.tf to state which providers and versions they need, but the provider configuration, region, credentials, aliases, belongs in the root module and is inherited. A module with its own provider block cannot be used with multiple regions or accounts, and cannot be removed cleanly from state. Pass provider aliases explicitly via the providers argument when a module genuinely needs a non-default one.
How do I version and share internal modules?

Put each in its own Git repository, or use a monorepo with tags, and source them with a pinned ?ref=v1.2.0. Tag releases with semantic versioning and treat an input rename as a breaking change, because it is. For larger organisations, a private Terraform registry gives proper version constraints and discoverability. Whatever you choose, pinning is the part that matters. An unpinned internal module is as risky as an unpinned external one.
How do I test a Terraform module?

Start with the cheap layers: terraform validate and terraform fmt -check in CI, plus tfsec or Checkov for security policy. Beyond that, the native terraform test framework runs assertions against plan or apply results using .tftest.hcl files, which is enough for most modules. Terratest, which drives real infrastructure from Go, is heavier but suited to modules where a genuine end-to-end check is worth the runtime and cost.

sections.title: What Are Data Sources?
paragraphs: Terraform data sources let you read information about infrastructure that already exists without telling Terraform to create, update, or destroy that infrastructure. They are one of the most important ideas for beginners because real Terraform projects rarely operate in a completely empty cloud account.
In practice, teams often have a mixture of new and existing resources:
Your Terraform code may need to discover those values before it can create anything new. That is the job of a data source.
A resource says, "Terraform, manage this object for me." A data source says, "Terraform, look this object up and give me its details."

That distinction is simple, but it changes how you design infrastructure code. If you need to launch an EC2 instance inside an existing VPC, you should not create a second VPC just because Terraform needs a VPC ID. Instead, you read the existing VPC with a data source and then feed that ID into your new resources.

sections.title: Why Data Sources Matter in Real Projects
paragraphs: Beginners sometimes start with examples where every resource is created from scratch in one directory. That is useful for learning syntax, but it is not how most production environments work.
In a real AWS account, infrastructure is usually shared and layered:
Your module often needs to connect to those shared building blocks. Data sources make that possible without taking ownership away from the original team.

They also improve portability. Instead of hardcoding values like AMI IDs or subnet IDs, you can make Terraform query AWS dynamically. That means your configuration can adapt across regions, accounts, or environments with fewer manual edits.

sections.title: Filtering Data Sources
paragraphs: Most useful data sources support filtering. Filters are how you narrow down the provider search until Terraform can identify the exact object or objects you want.
A common pattern uses one or more filter blocks:
When you combine filters, Terraform asks the provider to return objects matching all of them.
With image lookups, several results may match the same pattern. Setting most_recent = true tells Terraform to pick the newest one.
That is especially useful for AMIs because image IDs change frequently. You usually care about a stable naming pattern and the newest published version, not a fixed AMI ID that grows stale.
Poorly designed filters can make data sources unreliable. If your filter is too broad, Terraform may find the wrong object. If it is too narrow, the lookup may fail when naming conventions change.

sections.title: Data Sources vs Resources
paragraphs: This is the most important conceptual comparison in the tutorial.
A resource is part of Terraform's managed infrastructure graph. Terraform tracks it in state and may create, update, or delete it.
A data source is read-only. Terraform tracks the fact that the lookup exists in the dependency graph, but it does not own the remote object.
Use a resource when you want Terraform to manage the lifecycle of something:
Use a data source when the object already exists or is generated outside your configuration:
Ask yourself: Should Terraform own this object?
That rule prevents a lot of beginner confusion.

sections.title: Data Sources and Terraform State
paragraphs: Data sources do participate in Terraform's graph, but they behave differently from resources in state.
A key thing to remember is this:
Data sources are refreshed during planning.
That means every time you run terraform plan, Terraform asks the provider for fresh values. If the latest Ubuntu AMI changed since yesterday, your data source result can change too.
This is powerful, but it also means data-driven configurations can behave differently over time without any .tf file edits.
That is not a bug. It is the expected consequence of choosing a dynamic lookup.

Dynamic lookups reduce manual maintenance, but they can introduce change unexpectedly. In production, some teams prefer to pin values after testing, while others intentionally want the latest approved image every time.
The right choice depends on your operational model.

sections.title: Dependency Behavior with Data Sources
paragraphs: Terraform automatically understands dependencies when one object references another.
Because the security group references data.aws_vpc.main.id, Terraform knows it must resolve the VPC lookup before planning the security group.
The same principle works when data sources feed locals, modules, and outputs.
