If you hardcode an AMI ID, your configuration becomes tightly tied to one specific image in one region. That creates several problems:
With a data source, the configuration is more portable and easier to maintain.

Because most_recent = true is dynamic, a future terraform plan may choose a newer AMI and propose instance replacement. That may be desirable in a learning lab, but in production you should be intentional about when image updates happen.

sections.title: Another Example: Reading Existing Network Information
paragraphs: Data sources become even more valuable when your code integrates with a shared environment.
Imagine a VPC already exists, and your Terraform project should only create an EC2 instance inside that network.
Here, Terraform does not manage the VPC or subnets. It simply discovers them and uses them.
That pattern is extremely common in organizations with shared networking.

sections.title: Best Practices for Using Data Sources Well
paragraphs: Filtering by trusted tags, known owners, and consistent naming conventions is usually safer than matching vague patterns.
If something naturally changes over time or varies by region, a data source may be a better fit than a literal value.
Dynamic data is useful, but it also means the same configuration can plan differently next week. That is powerful, not magical. Treat it carefully.
Do not use data sources as a substitute for proper module boundaries. If your team should manage the resource, define it as a resource. If another team owns it, read it as data.
When you are new to Terraform, outputs help you see what the lookup actually returned:
That makes debugging much easier.

sections.title: Common Beginner Mistakes
paragraphs: A data block never creates a VPC, AMI, subnet, or identity. It only reads what already exists.
If your lookup is not specific enough, Terraform may fail or return something unexpected.
If the AMI ID, region, or availability zones vary, static values often become maintenance pain.
This is especially important for most_recent image lookups. If the data changes, your plan can change.

sections.title: Final Thoughts
paragraphs: Terraform data sources are the bridge between new infrastructure you want Terraform to manage and existing infrastructure or provider facts Terraform needs to read. Once you understand that boundary, many real-world Terraform patterns become much easier to reason about.
The mental model is simple:
If you use data sources thoughtfully, your Terraform code becomes more reusable, more environment-aware, and better aligned with how real cloud platforms are shared across teams.

sections.title: Frequently Asked Questions
paragraphs: What is a Terraform data source?

A read-only lookup. Where a resource block creates and manages something, a data block queries something that already exists and makes its attributes available. Typical uses are finding the latest AMI ID, reading an existing VPC created by another team, fetching the current AWS account ID, or pulling a secret from Secrets Manager at plan time. All without Terraform taking ownership of them.
What is the difference between a data source and a resource?

A resource is managed: Terraform creates it, tracks it in state, updates it when configuration changes, and destroys it when removed. A data source is only read: it appears in state as a cached result but Terraform never modifies or deletes the underlying object. Use a data source for anything owned elsewhere, and a resource for anything this configuration is responsible for.
How do I stop hardcoding AMI IDs?

Use the aws_ami data source with filters and most_recent = true, or read the AMI ID from the SSM public parameters that AWS publishes with the aws_ssm_parameter data source. Both resolve the current image at plan time, which removes a value that goes stale and becomes a security liability. Be aware this means a new AMI can trigger instance replacement, so pair it with a launch template and an Auto Scaling group rather than a bare instance if you want control over when that happens.
When are data sources evaluated?

During the plan, provided their arguments are known. If a data source depends on an attribute of a resource that does not yet exist, Terraform defers it to apply time and shows dependent values as (known after apply). This is why a data source that filters on a resource being created in the same run behaves differently from one querying pre-existing infrastructure, and why splitting such configurations into two applies is sometimes cleaner.
Can I use a data source to read another configuration's state?

Yes, with terraform_remote_state, which reads the outputs of another state file. It works, but it couples the two configurations tightly. The consumer breaks if the producer's outputs change, and it needs read access to the other state, which contains secrets. Many teams prefer publishing values to SSM Parameter Store and reading them back with a data source, which is a looser contract and avoids granting state access.
Why does my data source fail with "no matching results"?

The filters matched nothing, usually because of the region, the account, or a tag that does not exist. Data sources fail the plan rather than returning empty, which is deliberate. Continuing with a missing value would produce worse errors later. Check you are in the expected region and account with aws sts get-caller-identity, and test the equivalent CLI query directly to confirm the filters match something before debugging the Terraform side.

sections.title: Introduction & Overview
paragraphs: Choose between Terraform count and for_each: see why count's positional identity can destroy resources, when each is correct and how to migrate safely.
Two meta-arguments create multiple instances from one resource block. They look interchangeable and are not, and choosing wrongly is one of the most common ways to destroy infrastructure by accident.
The difference is how instances are identified.

sections.title: count
paragraphs: Three instances, addressed aws_instance.worker[0] through [2].
Reference them individually by index, or all at once with a splat:

sections.title: The problem with count
paragraphs: This is the part that matters, and it is worth understanding precisely.
Remove "artifacts" from the middle of that list and everything shifts down:
One removal, three resources destroyed. Terraform is behaving correctly, index [1] genuinely changed from artifacts to backups, but the result is that deleting one bucket destroys two unrelated ones.
On stateless resources this is wasteful. On databases, volumes, or anything holding data, it is an outage.

sections.title: for_each
paragraphs: for_each keys instances by a stable string instead:
Remove "artifacts" and exactly one resource is destroyed. Everything else is untouched, because nothing else's key changed.
A map is the more useful shape, because the key names the instance and the value carries its configuration:
Reference by key: aws_subnet.this["public-a"].id. For all of them, use a for expression. The splat syntax that works with count does not apply, because for_each produces a map rather than a list:
for_each needs a map or a set, so a list must be converted:
Never key on the index. { for i, s in var.subnets : i => s } reintroduces exactly the positional-identity problem for_each exists to solve.

sections.title: When count is still right
paragraphs: Conditional creation: still the idiomatic pattern:
Reference it as aws_s3_bucket.logs[0], and handle the zero case when referencing, one(aws_s3_bucket.logs[*].id) returns the value or null rather than erroring.
A genuine quantity of identical things, where the index carries no meaning and nothing distinguishes one from another. Three interchangeable workers, for instance.
Everything else should be for_each.

sections.title: Migrating from count to for_each
paragraphs: Changing the meta-argument changes every state address, so Terraform plans to destroy and recreate everything. Use moved blocks:
One per instance. Tedious, but it converts a rebuild into a no-op. Run a plan afterwards and confirm it is empty before applying.

sections.title: Final Thoughts
paragraphs: Default to for_each. Use count for conditional creation and for genuinely interchangeable quantities, and nowhere else. The question worth asking before choosing is simple: could an item ever be removed from the middle? If yes, positional identity will eventually destroy something you did not intend, and no amount of care at apply time will catch it.

sections.title: Frequently Asked Questions
paragraphs: What is the difference between count and for_each in Terraform?

count takes a number and identifies instances by position, [0], [1], [2]. for_each takes a map or set and identifies them by key, ["web"], ["api"]. That difference in identity determines what happens when the collection changes: with count, removing an item shifts every subsequent index and causes Terraform to destroy and recreate unrelated resources; with for_each, each instance is bound to its key, so removing one affects only that one.
Why did removing one item from my list destroy several resources?

Because you used count, which identifies resources by their position in the list. Removing the second of four items means index [1] now holds what used to be at [2], [2] holds what was at [3], and [3] no longer exists, so Terraform correctly plans to change two resources and destroy one. Switching to for_each with stable keys prevents this entirely, since identity no longer depends on ordering.
Should I always use for_each instead of count?

Nearly always, with two exceptions. Conditional creation reads more clearly as count = var.enabled ? 1 : 0, and a genuine quantity of interchangeable resources, three identical workers where nothing distinguishes them, is a legitimate use of count. Anything driven by a list that could gain or lose entries should use for_each.
How do I use for_each with a list?

You cannot directly, because for_each requires stable keys and a list has none. Convert a list of unique strings with toset(var.names), after which each.key and each.value are both the string. Convert a list of objects with a for expression keyed on a stable field, such as { for s in var.subnets : s.name => s }. Never key on the list index, which reintroduces the positional problem.
How do I create a resource conditionally in Terraform?

count = var.enabled ? 1 : 0. Zero instances means the resource is not created. Reference it as resource.name[0], and use one(resource.name[*].id) when the reference must tolerate the resource not existing, since indexing directly errors when count is zero. The same effect can be achieved with for_each over a map that is empty when disabled, which avoids index-based referencing entirely.
How do I convert existing resources from count to for_each?

Add a moved block for each instance, mapping the old indexed address to the new keyed one, from = aws_s3_bucket.this[0], to = aws_s3_bucket.this["logs"]. Without them Terraform sees every address change and plans a full destroy and recreate. It is tedious for a large set, but it turns a rebuild into a no-op. Always run a plan afterwards and confirm it reports no changes before applying.

paragraphs: Learn how the Terraform count meta-argument works: use count.index, build conditional resources, reference counted resources and know when count fits.

sections.title: What Is the count Meta-Argument?
paragraphs: The count meta-argument lets Terraform create multiple instances from a single resource block. Instead of copy-pasting the same EC2 instance, subnet, or IAM user block several times, you define one block and tell Terraform how many copies to make.
At its simplest, count looks like this:
Terraform expands that one block into three instances:
That indexing behavior is the foundation of count. Every instance is identified by a numeric position starting at zero.

count is called a meta-argument because it is not specific to one resource type. Many resources and modules can use it. It changes how Terraform interprets the block rather than configuring the cloud provider object itself.

sections.title: Why count Is Useful
paragraphs: Without count, repeating resources means repeating code. That creates several problems:
With count, you keep the declaration compact and let Terraform handle repetition.
A simple example is creating multiple nearly identical instances:
Now the number of instances can be changed by adjusting a variable instead of rewriting resource blocks.

sections.title: How count Works Internally
paragraphs: When Terraform sees count, it evaluates the expression to a whole number. If the result is 0, no instances are created. If the result is 1, exactly one instance exists. If the result is 5, Terraform creates five instances and assigns them indexes from 0 to 4.

sections.title: Final Thoughts
paragraphs: Terraform count is one of the easiest ways to reduce repetition. It helps you create multiple similar resources, work through lists with count.index, and toggle resources on or off with simple conditionals.

sections.title: Frequently Asked Questions
paragraphs: What does the count meta-argument do?

It creates multiple instances of a resource from one block, indexed from zero. Each instance gets an address like aws_instance.web[0], and count.index is available inside the block to differentiate them. It is the simplest way to create N identical things, and it is also the source of the most common Terraform footgun. See the next question.
Why does removing an item from a count list destroy other resources?

Because count identifies instances by position, not by value. Remove the second item from a list of four and everything after it shifts down an index, so Terraform sees [1] changing from one value to another, [2] changing, and [3] disappearing, and plans to destroy and recreate resources you never touched. On stateless resources this is merely wasteful; on anything with data attached it is an outage. This is the single strongest argument for for_each.
When should I use count instead of for_each?

Use count for a genuine quantity of identical things, three identical workers where the index carries no meaning, and for conditional creation with count = var.enabled ? 1 : 0, which remains the idiomatic pattern. Use for_each whenever the instances are distinguishable, because it keys them by a stable string so adding or removing one affects only that one. If the list you are counting over could ever have an element removed from the middle, use for_each.
How do I conditionally create a resource in Terraform?

count = var.create_bucket ? 1 : 0. Zero instances means the resource is not created. Reference it as aws_s3_bucket.this[0], and note that any reference must handle the zero case or the plan errors when the resource does not exist, which is where one() or a try() wrapper helps. for_each over a conditionally empty map achieves the same thing and avoids the index-based referencing.
How do I reference a resource created with count?

By index, aws_instance.web[0].id, or as a whole list with the splat expression aws_instance.web[*].id, which returns every instance's ID and is what you usually want for passing into a target group or a security group rule. Splat works cleanly even when count is zero, returning an empty list, which makes it safer than indexing directly in conditional cases.
Can I use count with modules?

Yes, count works on module blocks exactly as it does on resources, producing module.name[0]. The same positional-identity caveat applies and matters more, because recreating a module instance recreates every resource inside it. For anything beyond a simple conditional enable, for_each on the module block is the safer choice.

That difference is what makes for_each so valuable for real infrastructure.

sections.title: Why for_each Exists
paragraphs: If count already creates multiple resources, why does Terraform also need for_each?
Because many infrastructure collections are not really just "three copies." They are named things:
When the objects have their own identity, a name or key is a better model than a position in a list.
That is the core benefit of for_each: it gives each instance a stable logical identity.

sections.title: Why for_each Is Safer Than count for Named Items
paragraphs: The biggest practical benefit of for_each is stable identity.
Terraform tracks instances by those names. If you remove api, Terraform removes only the api instance. The app and worker instances keep their identity.
With count, the same collection might be tied to indexes [0], [1], and [2]. Removing the middle item can shift indexes and cause replacement of later resources.
That makes for_each a much better choice for long-lived named infrastructure.

sections.title: Best Practices for for_each
paragraphs: The key becomes the identity of the instance. Pick values that are stable and meaningful, such as environment names, team names, or bucket names.
If each resource has its own settings, a map or map of objects is usually the clearest model.
If your input starts as a list of objects, use a for expression to create a map keyed by a unique field.
Every key in for_each must be unique. If two objects generate the same key, Terraform cannot distinguish them.
Renaming a key is effectively changing instance identity. Terraform may destroy the old instance and create a new one.

For maps, each.key is the name and each.value is the configuration. Use the right one in the right place.
If keys depend on transient data, resource identity becomes fragile.
If the collection is conceptually dev, stage, and prod, forcing it into indexes is usually a sign that for_each is the better fit.

sections.title: Frequently Asked Questions
paragraphs: What is the difference between for_each and count?

count creates instances identified by a numeric index; for_each creates them identified by a string key from a map or set. That difference in identity is everything. With count, removing an item from the middle of a list shifts every subsequent index and causes Terraform to destroy and recreate unrelated resources. With for_each, each instance is bound to its key, so removing one affects only that one. Prefer for_each for anything where instances are distinguishable.
Should I always use for_each instead of count?

Nearly always, with two exceptions. Conditional creation reads better as count = var.enabled ? 1 : 0, and a genuine quantity of truly interchangeable resources, three identical workers where nothing distinguishes them, is a legitimate count. Everything else, especially anything driven by a list that could change, belongs in for_each.
How do I use for_each with a list?

You cannot directly, for_each requires a map or a set of strings, because it needs stable keys. Convert with toset(var.names) for a list of unique strings, after which each.key and each.value are both the string. For a list of objects, project it into a map first with a for expression keyed on something stable and unique, such as { for s in var.subnets : s.name => s }. Never key on an index, which reintroduces the problem for_each exists to solve.
What is the difference between each.key and each.value?

With a set of strings they are the same value. With a map, each.key is the map key and each.value is the corresponding value, which is what makes a map of objects the most useful shape. The key names the instance and the object carries its configuration. Referencing the instance later uses the key: aws_subnet.this["public-a"].id.
Why do I get "Invalid for_each argument" at plan time?

Because the keys are not known until apply. for_each keys must be determinable during planning, so a map derived from an attribute of a resource that does not exist yet, an ID assigned on creation, for instance, fails with this error. The fix is to key on something static, such as a variable or a literal name, and keep the unknown value inside the map's value rather than its key.
How do I reference resources created with for_each?

By key: aws_subnet.this["public-a"].id. For all of them, use a for expression such as [for s in aws_subnet.this : s.id], or values(aws_subnet.this)[*].id. The splat syntax that works with count does not apply directly to for_each resources, because they form a map rather than a list. This is a common stumbling block when converting a resource from one to the other.

sections.title: Introduction & Overview
paragraphs: Learn Terraform expressions: types, references, conditionals, for expressions, key function categories, try and can, and testing in terraform console.
HCL is a configuration language with a real expression system underneath it. Most of what separates a readable Terraform configuration from a repetitive one is knowing which expressions exist.
There is no user-defined function support. You use the built-in library, composed with for expressions and locals.

sections.title: Types
paragraphs: The list-versus-set distinction matters for for_each, which needs a map or a set because it requires stable keys. Converting with toset() is a routine step.

Terraform converts types automatically where it can, a number used in a string context becomes a string, which is convenient and occasionally surprising when a value you expected to be numeric arrives quoted.

sections.title: Referencing things
paragraphs: Interpolation embeds an expression in a string: "${var.project}-${var.environment}". Do not wrap a value that is already a string, name = var.name, not name = "${var.name}".

codeBlock.code:
var.environment                    # input variable
local.name_prefix                  # local value
aws_instance.web.id                # resource attribute
aws_instance.web[0].id             # count instance
aws_subnet.this["public-a"].id     # for_each instance
module.vpc.vpc_id                  # module output
data.aws_ami.al2023.id             # data source
each.key / each.value              # inside for_each
count.index                        # inside count

sections.title: Conditionals
paragraphs: Both branches must return the same type. Chaining more than two levels becomes unreadable quickly. A lookup() against a map of per-environment values is usually clearer:

codeBlock.code:
instance_type = var.environment == "prod" ? "m6i.large" : "t3.micro"
count         = var.enabled ? 1 : 0

sections.title: for expressions
paragraphs: The most powerful construct in the language. It transforms one collection into another.

Square brackets produce a list or tuple; braces produce a map and require the key => value form. The optional if clause filters. There is no separate filter function, and this is the idiomatic way to do it.
Filtering and transforming happen in one pass, which is why a for expression usually replaces what would be several steps elsewhere.

codeBlock.code:
# list -> list
[for name in var.names : upper(name)]

# list -> list, filtered
[for s in var.subnets : s.id if s.public]

# list of objects -> map, the for_each pattern
{ for s in var.subnets : s.name => s }

# map -> map
{ for k, v in var.tags : lower(k) => v }

sections.title: The function categories worth knowing
paragraphs: Strings: join, split, format, lower, upper, replace, trimspace, substr, startswith, endswith
Collections: merge, concat, flatten, lookup, keys, values, contains, length, distinct, toset
Numeric: min, max, ceil, floor, abs
Encoding: jsonencode, jsondecode, base64encode, yamlencode
jsonencode is how IAM policies should be written, rather than as heredoc strings. It validates structure and handles escaping:
Network: cidrsubnet, cidrhost, cidrnetmask
Deriving subnet ranges beats hand-calculating them, and it keeps the arithmetic correct when the VPC CIDR changes.
Filesystem and templates: file, templatefile
Keep scripts in real files rather than heredocs. They get syntax highlighting, linting, and a sensible diff.

codeBlock.code:
join(",", var.subnet_ids)
format("%s-%03d", var.prefix, count.index)    # zero-padded, sorts correctly
lower(replace(var.name, "_", "-"))            # normalise for S3 naming rules

sections.title: try, can and one
paragraphs: Three functions for handling values that might not exist:

lookup(map, key, default) handles a straightforward map access with a fallback. try() is broader, catching type errors and missing attributes on nested objects. can() is what you want inside a validation block, since it returns a boolean rather than failing.

codeBlock.code:
try(var.config.timeout, 30)            # first expression that succeeds
can(regex("^prod-", var.name))         # returns bool instead of erroring
one(aws_instance.web[*].id)            # single value or null, for count = 0/1

sections.title: Test expressions before you apply
paragraphs: terraform console has access to your variables, locals, data sources and state. It is read-only and safe to run against production, and it is by far the fastest way to work out why an expression is not producing what you expect. Much better than adding an output and running a plan.

codeBlock.code: terraform console

sections.title: Final Thoughts
paragraphs: Two things carry most of the weight here: the for expression, which turns lists into the maps for_each needs and filters in the same pass, and terraform console, which removes guesswork entirely. Learn those two and the function library becomes something you look up rather than memorise.

sections.title: Frequently Asked Questions
paragraphs: How do I test a Terraform expression without applying?

Use terraform console, an interactive prompt with access to your variables, locals, data sources and current state. Type an expression and it prints the result immediately. It is read-only and safe to run against production, and it answers "why is this not producing what I expect" far faster than adding a temporary output and running a plan. It is the single most underused Terraform command.
How do I write a conditional in Terraform?

With the ternary operator: var.env == "prod" ? "m6i.large" : "t3.micro". Both branches must return the same type. For conditional resource creation, use count = var.enabled ? 1 : 0. When you find yourself chaining more than two conditions, replace it with a map of values and lookup(map, key, default), which is considerably easier to read and to extend.
What is a for expression and when do I use it?

It transforms one collection into another, with optional filtering: [for s in var.subnets : s.id if s.public]. Square brackets produce a list, braces produce a map using key => value syntax. The most important use is converting a list into the map that for_each requires, since for_each needs stable keys. There is no separate filter function in Terraform. The if clause of a for expression is how filtering is done.
How do I merge maps or combine tags in Terraform?

merge(local.common_tags, { Name = "web-server" }), where later arguments win on key conflicts. This is the standard tagging pattern: define organisation-wide tags once in a locals block and merge per-resource additions at each use site. Many providers also support default_tags at the provider level, which applies tags automatically to every resource. Combining both gives you provider-wide defaults plus per-resource specifics with no repetition.
What is the difference between try, can and lookup?

lookup(map, key, default) retrieves a value from a map with a fallback when the key is missing. try(expr, fallback) evaluates expressions in order and returns the first that succeeds, handling a wider range of failures including type errors and missing attributes on nested objects. can(expr) returns a boolean instead of erroring, which is what makes it suitable inside a variable validation block where you need a condition rather than a value.
Can I write my own functions in Terraform?

Not in Terraform itself. The function library is fixed and there is no user-defined function support. The idiomatic substitute is a locals block, which lets you name a complex expression once and reuse it everywhere, giving most of the readability benefit. For genuinely complex logic, either reshape the input data so the expression becomes simple, or move the computation outside Terraform and pass the result in as a variable.

paragraphs: How do I join strings in Terraform?

Use interpolation for simple cases, "${var.project}-${var.environment}", and the join() function when combining a list, as in join(",", var.subnet_ids). Avoid wrapping a value that is already a string in interpolation: name = "${var.name}" should just be name = var.name, and terraform fmt will not fix it but linters flag it.
What is the difference between format() and string interpolation?

Interpolation is more readable for straightforward concatenation. format() earns its place when you need padding, number formatting or a reusable template, format("%s-%03d", var.prefix, count.index) produces zero-padded names that sort correctly, which plain interpolation cannot do. formatlist() applies the same template across a list, which is useful for generating a set of names in one expression.

A common normalisation is lower(replace(var.name, "_", "-")). Doing this in a locals block once, rather than at each use site, keeps the convention in one place.
How do I check whether a string contains a substring?

can(regex("pattern", var.string)) returns a boolean without failing when there is no match, which is what you want in a condition. regex() on its own errors if the pattern does not match, so it is only appropriate when a non-match should fail the plan, which makes it genuinely useful inside a variable validation block. startswith() and endswith() cover the simpler cases more legibly.
How do I split a string into a list?

split(",", var.csv_value) produces a list from a delimited string, which is the usual way to accept a comma-separated value from an environment variable or a CI parameter. Combine with trimspace() inside a for expression if the input may contain spaces around the delimiters, since split does not trim.

terraform console gives an interactive prompt with access to your variables, locals, data sources and state, so you can evaluate an expression against real values rather than guessing. It is the fastest way to work out why a function is not producing what you expect, and it is read-only, so it is safe to run against production state.

sections.title: Frequently Asked Questions
paragraphs: What is the difference between a list, a set and a map in Terraform?

A list is ordered and allows duplicates, indexed by position. A set is unordered with no duplicates, and cannot be indexed. A map is a collection of key-value pairs with unique string keys. The distinction matters for for_each, which requires a map or a set of strings because it needs stable keys. A list must be converted with toset() or projected into a map first.
How do I merge two maps?

merge(local.common_tags, { Name = "web-server" }) combines them, with later arguments winning on key conflicts. This is the standard tagging pattern: a base map of organisation-wide tags merged with per-resource additions. merge() accepts any number of maps, so layering defaults, environment values and resource specifics in one expression works cleanly.
How do I transform a list into a map for for_each?

Use a for expression: { for s in var.subnets : s.name => s } produces a map keyed on each object's name. The key must be unique and stable, never derive it from the list index, since that reintroduces exactly the positional-identity problem for_each exists to avoid. If no field is naturally unique, combine two, such as "${s.az}-${s.tier}".
What does flatten() do and when do I need it?

It collapses nested lists into a single flat list. It is most often needed when a for expression produces a list of lists. For example generating every combination of subnets and availability zones, and you want one flat collection to iterate over. Pair it with a for expression producing objects, then project into a map for for_each, which is the standard pattern for generating a matrix of resources.
What is the difference between lookup() and try()?

lookup(map, key, default) retrieves a map value with a fallback if the key is absent. try() evaluates a series of expressions and returns the first that succeeds, which handles a broader range of failures including type errors and missing attributes on objects. Use lookup for a straightforward map access with a default; use try when the expression itself might be invalid, such as reaching into a nested structure that may not exist.
How do I filter a list in Terraform?

With a for expression and an if clause: [for s in var.subnets : s.id if s.public]. The same syntax builds filtered maps by using the key => value form. There is no dedicated filter function, and the for expression is the idiomatic approach. It also handles transformation at the same time, so filtering and mapping happen in one pass.

sections.title: What Are Dynamic Blocks?
paragraphs: Terraform dynamic blocks let you generate repeated nested blocks inside a resource, data source, provider, or provisioner configuration. They are useful when the block you want to repeat is not a top-level resource but a nested configuration block such as ingress, egress, statement, or another provider-defined structure.
A normal resource block with count or for_each repeats the entire resource. A dynamic block repeats just one nested portion inside the resource.
That is the key idea.

For example, an AWS security group can contain multiple ingress blocks. If the number of ingress rules varies by environment or is driven by input data, hardcoding every ingress block can become repetitive. A dynamic block lets Terraform generate those nested blocks from a collection.

sections.title: Frequently Asked Questions
paragraphs: What is a dynamic block in Terraform?

A way to generate repeated nested blocks from a collection. Where a resource takes multiple ingress or setting blocks, a dynamic block iterates over a list or map and emits one for each element, using content to define the shape and <name>.value to access the current item. It removes the need to copy a nested block five times with slightly different values.
When should I use a dynamic block?

When the number of nested blocks genuinely varies. Security group rules driven by a variable, tags on a resource type that uses block syntax, environment settings whose count differs by caller. Do not use one for a fixed, small number of blocks: two hand-written ingress blocks are far easier to read than a dynamic block over a two-element list, and readability matters more than avoiding repetition at that scale.
What is the difference between a dynamic block and for_each on a resource?

for_each on a resource creates multiple resources; a dynamic block creates multiple nested blocks inside one resource. Five subnets means for_each on aws_subnet. Five ingress rules inside one security group means a dynamic "ingress" block. Choosing the wrong one produces either a single resource that should have been several, or several resources that should have been one.
Why is my dynamic block producing nothing?

The collection it iterates over is empty, which produces zero blocks and no error. That is usually correct behaviour, but it surprises people who expected a default. Check the value with terraform console and confirm it is populated. The other frequent cause is referencing the wrong iterator name. Inside dynamic "ingress" the variable is ingress.value unless you override it with iterator.
Can I nest dynamic blocks?

Yes, and it is occasionally necessary for deeply structured resources. It is also where Terraform configuration becomes genuinely hard to read, so treat a second level of nesting as a signal to reconsider the data structure. Flattening the input into a list of fully-formed objects usually produces a simpler configuration than two nested loops. Run terraform console or a plan and read the rendered output when nesting, because the mistakes are not obvious from the source.
Should I prefer security group rule resources over dynamic ingress blocks?

Often, yes. Separate aws_vpc_security_group_ingress_rule resources with for_each give each rule its own state address, so adding or removing one shows as a single change rather than a rewrite of the whole security group, and a description per rule is preserved cleanly. Dynamic blocks inside aws_security_group remain valid, but the standalone rule resources produce clearer plans on anything that changes regularly.

sections.title: What Are Terraform Workspaces?
paragraphs: Terraform workspaces let you use the same Terraform configuration with multiple separate state instances. The most common reason is to represent different environments such as dev, staging, and prod without duplicating all of your .tf files.
A workspace does not create a new directory or a new configuration. It changes which state Terraform is currently using for the same configuration.
That means one codebase can be applied more than once while keeping each environment's state separate.

sections.title: Workspaces and State
paragraphs: One of the most important facts about workspaces is this:
Each workspace has its own state file or state namespace.
That means Terraform keeps separate records of managed resources for:
and any other workspaces you create.
This separation is what prevents Terraform from confusing dev resources with prod resources when using the same code.
Terraform decisions are based on state. If multiple environments shared exactly the same state accidentally, Terraform would not be able to model them independently.
Workspaces solve that by splitting state while reusing code.

The exact storage behavior depends on the backend. With local state, workspace state is stored locally in different paths. With remote backends, the backend typically stores workspace state in separate logical locations.
The details vary, but the high-level idea remains the same: each workspace has its own isolated state context.

sections.title: Limitations of Workspaces
paragraphs: This is where many beginner misunderstandings happen.
Terraform workspaces are useful, but they are not a full replacement for separate state design, separate backends, or separate repositories in every situation.
Workspaces assume a mostly shared configuration. If environments differ dramatically, the configuration can become filled with conditionals and exceptions.
Workspaces usually separate state within the same backend configuration. Some organizations want stronger isolation, separate credentials, or separate backend stores per environment.
If an operator selects the wrong workspace and runs apply, changes may hit the wrong environment. That risk becomes more serious in production.
Large systems often prefer dedicated state, separate pipelines, separate directories, or separate repositories for stronger boundaries between environments.

sections.title: Workspaces vs Separate Directories or Repositories

sections.title: Frequently Asked Questions
paragraphs: What are Terraform workspaces for?

A workspace gives one configuration multiple independent state files, so the same code can manage several parallel instances of the same infrastructure. Every configuration starts in a workspace called default. They are genuinely useful for short-lived parallel copies, a per-developer sandbox, a per-pull-request preview environment, where the infrastructure is identical and only needs isolating.
Should I use workspaces for dev, staging and production?

Generally no, despite it being the obvious first idea. Workspaces share one configuration and one backend, so environments cannot differ structurally, the same credentials reach all of them, and it is uncomfortably easy to run an apply against production because you forgot to check terraform workspace show. Separate directories or separate repositories with separate backends give real isolation, allow environments to differ, and let production credentials be scoped to production alone.
How do I know which workspace I am in?

terraform workspace show prints it, and terraform workspace list marks the current one with an asterisk. Because nothing else in the output reminds you, showing it in your shell prompt is worth setting up if you use workspaces regularly. Within configuration, terraform.workspace returns the name, commonly used to derive resource names or select a map of per-workspace values.
How do I use the workspace name in my configuration?

terraform.workspace is available anywhere as a string, so name = "app-${terraform.workspace}" gives per-workspace resource names. A common pattern is a map of settings keyed by workspace with a lookup and a default, which lets a sandbox use small instances while a shared workspace uses larger ones. Keep this light. Heavy branching on workspace name is a sign the environments should be separate configurations.
Where is state stored for each workspace?

In the same backend, under a separate path. With the S3 backend, non-default workspaces are stored under a env:/<workspace>/ prefix alongside your configured key, while default uses the key directly. They are isolated from each other but share the bucket and its access controls, which is precisely why workspaces do not give production the credential separation it should have.
How do I delete a workspace?

Destroy its resources first with terraform destroy while it is selected, then switch away and run terraform workspace delete <name>. Terraform refuses to delete a workspace whose state is non-empty unless you force it, and forcing leaves orphaned infrastructure nobody is tracking. For ephemeral preview environments, wire the destroy-then-delete sequence into the pipeline that tears the environment down.

sections.title: Introduction & Overview
paragraphs: Configure the Terraform AWS provider, authenticate without long-lived keys using assume role and OIDC, manage regions and accounts, and tag everything.

The AWS provider is the most used Terraform provider by a wide margin. The mechanics of writing resources are covered in the pages below. This page is about the decisions that surround them: how Terraform authenticates, how you handle more than one region or account, and the conventions that stop an estate becoming unmanageable.

sections.title: Provider configuration
paragraphs: Two things worth doing from the start.

Pin the provider version with a pessimistic constraint. AWS provider major versions carry breaking changes. The v4 release split aws_s3_bucket inline blocks into separate resources, which broke a great many configurations that had not pinned.

Use default_tags. Every resource that supports tagging gets these automatically, with no repetition. It is the cheapest way to make cost allocation and ownership work, and retrofitting tags across an existing estate is tedious.

sections.title: Authentication
paragraphs: Terraform uses the standard AWS credential chain, so it picks up whatever the AWS CLI would. In order of preference:
OIDC federation in CI: the right answer for pipelines. No stored credentials at all:
The pipeline exchanges a signed token for temporary credentials, and the role's trust policy restricts which repository and branch may do so. Nothing long-lived exists to leak or rotate.
A named profile locally:
Assume-role in the provider block, which is how one configuration manages several accounts.
What not to do: hardcode access_key and secret_key in the provider block. They end up in version control, and they are unnecessary in every environment where Terraform actually runs.
Always confirm which identity you are using before applying:
Pointing at the wrong account is the most expensive Terraform mistake available, and nothing in the plan output warns you.

sections.title: Multiple regions and accounts
paragraphs: A provider block covers one region and one account. For more, use aliases:
That ACM example is the one almost everyone meets. CloudFront only accepts certificates from us-east-1 regardless of where the rest of the stack lives.
For modules that need a non-default provider, pass it explicitly:
Modules must never declare their own provider block. They declare required_providers and inherit configuration from the root.

sections.title: Structuring an AWS estate
paragraphs: The pattern that scales:

Each environment is a root module calling shared modules with different values. State is separate per environment, so a staging mistake cannot touch production state, and credentials can be scoped so a staging pipeline cannot reach production at all.

Split by change frequency, not just by environment. Networking changes rarely and is shared; application infrastructure changes constantly. Keeping them in one state means every deploy plans against the whole VPC and a mistake has a wider blast radius. Put the VPC in its own configuration and expose IDs as outputs.

codeBlock.code:
environments/
├── production/     # own backend key, own state, own credentials
├── staging/
└── dev/
modules/
├── network/
├── application/
└── data/

sections.title: Reading values from elsewhere
paragraphs: To consume another configuration's output, terraform_remote_state works but couples the two tightly and requires read access to state, which contains secrets.
A looser alternative is publishing to SSM Parameter Store and reading it back:
Also stop hardcoding AMI IDs. AWS publishes current images as public SSM parameters:

sections.title: Things that bite
paragraphs: Resource replacement on immutable attributes. Subnet CIDRs, availability zones, RDS engine versions in some cases. The plan shows -/+ with a # forces replacement annotation. Read every plan for that marker before applying to anything stateful.
Eventual consistency. IAM in particular propagates slowly, so a role created and used in the same apply occasionally fails. Explicit depends_on helps; a retry sometimes is the pragmatic answer.
Provider v4 S3 changes. Versioning, encryption and public access blocks are now separate resources rather than inline blocks. Older tutorials will not work.
Service quotas. Terraform surfaces the API error, which often reads as a permissions problem. Check quotas before assuming IAM.

sections.title: Final Thoughts
paragraphs: The Terraform part of AWS work is rarely the hard part. What determines whether an estate stays manageable is the surrounding decisions: pin the provider, tag by default, authenticate with roles rather than keys, keep state separate per environment, and split configurations by how often they change. Get those right early and the resource blocks look after themselves.

sections.title: Frequently Asked Questions
paragraphs: How should Terraform authenticate to AWS?

Through the standard credential chain, never with keys hardcoded in the provider block. Locally, use a named profile via AWS_PROFILE or AWS SSO. In CI, use OIDC federation. The pipeline exchanges a short-lived signed token for temporary credentials through an IAM role whose trust policy restricts which repository and branch may assume it. That removes long-lived credentials entirely, so there is nothing to rotate and nothing useful in a leaked log.
How do I use Terraform across multiple AWS regions?

Declare additional provider blocks with an alias, then set provider = aws.us_east_1 on resources that belong in the other region. The case everyone meets is ACM certificates for CloudFront, which must be issued in us-east-1 regardless of where the rest of the infrastructure lives. To use an aliased provider inside a module, pass it explicitly through the providers argument. Modules should never declare their own provider configuration.
How do I manage multiple AWS accounts with Terraform?

Use assume_role in the provider block, pointing at a role in the target account, with aliases when one configuration spans several accounts. More commonly, keep each account's infrastructure in its own root configuration with its own backend and credentials, which gives genuine isolation. A pipeline for staging then physically cannot reach production. AWS Organizations plus IAM Identity Center makes the role structure straightforward.
Why does Terraform want to replace my AWS resource instead of updating it?

Because you changed an attribute AWS cannot modify in place: a subnet's CIDR block, an instance's availability zone, certain database engine settings. The plan marks it -/+ and annotates the specific attribute with # forces replacement, so the cause is always stated. On stateless resources this is harmless; on anything storing data it is destructive. Protect critical resources with lifecycle { prevent_destroy = true } so a replacement cannot be applied accidentally.
How do I tag all my AWS resources consistently?

Use default_tags in the provider block, which applies the tags to every resource that supports tagging, with no repetition. Add per-resource tags normally and they merge with the defaults. This is the cheapest way to make cost allocation, ownership and automated cleanup work, and it is considerably easier to set up at the start than to retrofit across an existing estate.
Should the VPC and the application be in the same Terraform configuration?

Usually not. Networking changes rarely and is shared by many workloads; application infrastructure changes constantly. Combining them means every application deploy plans against the whole network, the blast radius of a mistake is larger, and applies are slower. Put the VPC in its own configuration, expose IDs as outputs, and consume them from application configurations through a data source or a value published to SSM Parameter Store.

sections.title: Project Overview
paragraphs: In this lesson, you are building the network foundation for the rest of the AWS project. The goal is a custom VPC with both public and private subnets. Later lessons will place an EC2 web server in a public subnet and store static assets in S3, but neither of those pieces should come first. Good cloud design starts with the network.
The VPC will include:

That architecture is common because it separates resources by exposure level. Public subnets are for components that must accept traffic from the internet, such as a bastion host, load balancer, or simple demo web server. Private subnets are for application servers, databases, or internal services that should not receive direct inbound traffic from the public internet.
Even if your first Terraform project is small, learning this pattern now pays off later. Most real AWS environments reuse the same ideas repeatedly.

A subnet becomes “public” when its route table sends outbound internet traffic to an Internet Gateway and resources inside it can receive public IP addresses. A subnet stays “private” when it does not expose that direct path.
Private resources often still need outbound internet access. For example:
A NAT gateway gives those private resources outbound internet connectivity without opening inbound access from the internet.

You will spread subnets across multiple AZs by using the AWS availability zone data source. This is good practice because it prepares the environment for high availability. Even if you launch only one EC2 instance today, you are learning a production-friendly network layout.

sections.title: Frequently Asked Questions
paragraphs: Should I write my own VPC module or use the community one?

Use the community terraform-aws-modules/vpc/aws module for anything real. VPC networking has a large number of interdependent pieces. Subnets across availability zones, route tables and associations, internet and NAT gateways, endpoints, flow logs, and the module handles combinations that take a long time to get right by hand. Writing your own is a genuinely useful learning exercise, and rarely the best production choice.
How do I create subnets across multiple availability zones?

Query the available zones with the aws_availability_zones data source rather than hardcoding names, then create subnets with for_each over a map keyed on a stable name. Use cidrsubnet() to carve the ranges from the VPC CIDR so they are derived rather than hand-calculated. Avoid count with an index into the AZ list, if AWS changes zone ordering or you remove one, positional identity causes unrelated subnets to be recreated.
How many NAT gateways should Terraform create?

One per availability zone for production, since a NAT gateway is zonal and losing its AZ takes outbound access with it. The community module exposes single_nat_gateway and one_nat_gateway_per_az to control this, and using a single gateway in non-production is a reasonable saving. Be aware NAT gateways are frequently the largest networking cost on an AWS bill, so add free S3 and DynamoDB gateway endpoints in the same configuration.
Why does changing a subnet CIDR want to destroy and recreate it?

Because a subnet's CIDR block is immutable. AWS provides no way to change it in place, so Terraform must replace the resource. The plan shows -/+ with a "forces replacement" annotation. Anything inside that subnet is affected, so treat CIDR changes as a migration rather than an edit. This is why sizing the VPC and its subnets generously at creation matters: a /20 per subnet costs nothing extra and avoids the problem entirely.
How do I tag subnets for EKS or load balancers?

The AWS Load Balancer Controller and EKS discover where to place resources from subnet tags, kubernetes.io/role/elb set to 1 on public subnets and kubernetes.io/role/internal-elb on private ones, plus a cluster ownership tag. The community VPC module accepts public_subnet_tags and private_subnet_tags for exactly this. Missing tags produce an Ingress that sits in pending with no clear error, which is a slow thing to diagnose.
Should the VPC live in the same Terraform state as my application?

Usually not. Networking changes rarely and is shared by many workloads, while application infrastructure changes constantly. Keeping them together means every application deploy plans against the whole VPC and a mistake has a larger blast radius. Put the VPC in its own configuration and expose IDs via outputs, then consume them from application configurations with a data source or by reading a parameter from SSM.

sections.title: Frequently Asked Questions
paragraphs: How do I avoid hardcoding an AMI ID in Terraform?

Use the aws_ami data source with owner and name filters plus most_recent = true, or read AWS's published SSM public parameters with the aws_ssm_parameter data source, /aws/service/ami-amazon-linux-latest/al2023-ami-kernel-default-x86_64 resolves the current Amazon Linux image. Both remove a value that goes stale and becomes a security liability. Note that a new AMI then triggers instance replacement, so pair this with a launch template and an Auto Scaling group if you want control over when that happens.
Should I create EC2 instances directly or use a launch template?

Use a launch template with an Auto Scaling group for anything that matters, even at a desired capacity of one. A bare aws_instance is a pet: if it fails, nothing replaces it, and every change risks manual repair. A launch template plus an Auto Scaling group makes replacement routine and gives you rolling updates via instance refresh. Reserve standalone instances for genuinely one-off or experimental work.
How do I pass startup configuration to an instance?

Through user_data, rendered with the templatefile() function so values can be interpolated from Terraform. Use user_data_replace_on_change = true if you want a change to the script to replace the instance, since by default a modified user_data does not affect a running instance. It only executes on first boot. For anything substantial, bake the configuration into an AMI with Packer instead, which makes instances start ready and shortens boot time.
Why does Terraform want to replace my instance when I only changed a tag?

It usually does not, and a replacement means something else changed. Most often the AMI ID resolved by a data source, or an attribute that is immutable such as the availability zone, subnet or certain instance metadata options. Read the plan carefully: Terraform annotates the specific attribute with "forces replacement", which names the cause precisely. If it is an AMI refresh you did not intend, pin the AMI or add ignore_changes to the lifecycle block.
How do I attach an IAM role to an EC2 instance in Terraform?

Create an aws_iam_role with a trust policy allowing ec2.amazonaws.com, attach the permission policies, then create an aws_iam_instance_profile referencing the role and set iam_instance_profile on the instance or launch template. The instance profile is the piece people miss. An EC2 instance cannot reference a role directly, and forgetting it produces credentials errors inside the instance that look unrelated to Terraform.
How do I manage EBS volumes with Terraform?

The root volume is configured inline with a root_block_device block; additional volumes are separate aws_ebs_volume resources attached with aws_volume_attachment. Use gp3 rather than gp2, since it is cheaper and faster with performance independent of size. Set encrypted = true, or better, enable EBS encryption by default at the account level so no configuration can forget it. Note that additional volumes do not delete on termination by default, which is usually what you want but does leave orphans if instances are replaced often.

sections.title: Continuing the AWS Project
paragraphs: So far, the project has a network layer and a public EC2 web server. The next useful component is object storage. In AWS, that means S3.

In this lesson, you will create an S3 bucket that stores static assets such as HTML, CSS, JavaScript, images, and downloads. The tutorial goes a bit further than “create a bucket” because real buckets need policy and lifecycle decisions too.
By the end, your S3 configuration will include:

This lesson intentionally uses a public static-asset pattern because it is easy to understand and test. In production, many teams prefer CloudFront in front of S3 instead of a directly public bucket, but learning the underlying S3 pieces is still valuable.

sections.title: Why S3 Belongs in This Project
paragraphs: An EC2 web server is good for dynamic pages or server-hosted apps, but it is inefficient to store every image, CSS file, or downloadable document on the instance itself. S3 is a better fit because it gives you:
Even if the EC2 server disappears, the bucket and its objects remain. That decoupling is one of the big operational wins of cloud architecture.

sections.title: The Bucket Naming Problem
paragraphs: S3 bucket names must be globally unique across AWS. That means a name like devopslesson-assets may already be taken by another account anywhere in the world.
Terraform solves this neatly with the random_id resource from the Random provider.

sections.title: Bucket Ownership Controls
paragraphs: Modern AWS S3 setups often use explicit ownership controls.

It helps ensure the bucket owner remains the preferred owner of uploaded objects, which avoids confusing access patterns later. In multi-account or multi-uploader environments, ownership rules matter a lot.
For a simple tutorial, you may not feel the impact immediately, but it is worth learning because modern S3 configuration is more explicit than older examples you may see online.

sections.title: Public Access Block Configuration
paragraphs: S3 public access settings confuse many beginners because they interact with both ACLs and bucket policies.

For this tutorial, the bucket should allow public read access through a bucket policy so static files can be served openly. That means the public access block cannot completely forbid public policies.
This is one of those cases where context matters. If you were building a private application bucket, you would likely lock these values down much harder.

  bucket = aws_s3_bucket.assets.id

  block_public_acls       = true
  ignore_public_acls      = true
  block_public_policy     = false
  restrict_public_buckets = false
}

sections.title: Frequently Asked Questions
paragraphs: Why does my S3 bucket configuration need so many separate resources?

Because the AWS provider split what was once a set of inline blocks on aws_s3_bucket into standalone resources, aws_s3_bucket_versioning, aws_s3_bucket_server_side_encryption_configuration, aws_s3_bucket_public_access_block, aws_s3_bucket_lifecycle_configuration and others. Older tutorials showing versioning or encryption inline are written for the pre-v4 provider and will not work. Each setting is now its own resource referencing the bucket by ID.
How do I make a bucket private and keep it that way?

Create an aws_s3_bucket_public_access_block with all four settings true, which is a hard override that no bucket policy can bypass. Combine it with aws_s3_bucket_ownership_controls set to BucketOwnerEnforced, which disables ACLs entirely. Object ACLs were behind most historic S3 exposure incidents. For content that genuinely must be public, front the private bucket with CloudFront using an Origin Access Control rather than opening the bucket.
How do I stop Terraform from deleting a bucket that contains objects?

By default AWS refuses to delete a non-empty bucket and the destroy fails, which is a useful accident. force_destroy = true makes Terraform empty it first, which is convenient for ephemeral test buckets and dangerous anywhere else. Set it deliberately and never on anything holding real data. For production, add lifecycle { prevent_destroy = true } so Terraform refuses any plan that would remove it.
How do I configure lifecycle rules in Terraform?

With aws_s3_bucket_lifecycle_configuration, containing rule blocks with transition and expiration actions. Add an abort_incomplete_multipart_upload rule to every bucket. Failed multipart uploads leave parts that are billed as storage but do not appear in a normal listing, and teams discover them years later as an unexplained cost. If versioning is enabled, include noncurrent_version_expiration or old versions accumulate indefinitely.
Should I use a bucket policy or IAM policies?

Within one account, IAM policies on the principals are sufficient and simpler. Use a bucket policy for cross-account access, for conditions that must apply to every caller regardless of their IAM, such as denying any request not over HTTPS, and for granting access to AWS services like CloudFront. A common mistake is writing both when only IAM is needed, which doubles the places a permission can be wrong.
How do I manage the S3 bucket that holds my Terraform state?

Not in the configuration that uses it, since the bucket must exist before terraform init can store state there. Create it in a small separate configuration with local state, or once via the CLI. Enable versioning so a bad state write can be recovered, enable encryption, block all public access, and restrict who can read it. State contains secrets in plain text. Keep that bootstrap configuration in version control even though its own state is local; it changes rarely.

sections.title: What Are Terraform Provisioners?
paragraphs: Provisioners are Terraform features that let you run scripts or copy files as part of resource creation or destruction. They sit at the edge between infrastructure provisioning and machine configuration.
In plain English, provisioners answer requests like:

Terraform introduced provisioners in its early 0.x releases, long before Terraform 1.0. They have been part of the tool for years, which is why you still see them in older blog posts, legacy codebases, and interview questions.

But there is a crucial catch: HashiCorp recommends against relying on provisioners for normal infrastructure design. They still exist, and they are sometimes useful, but they are intentionally treated as a last resort.
That tension is what makes this topic important. You need to understand both how provisioners work and why experienced Terraform users try to avoid them.

sections.title: Why Provisioners Feel Attractive at First
paragraphs: Provisioners are appealing because they look like a shortcut.
Imagine you create an EC2 instance and then want to:
A provisioner can do all of that. That sounds convenient, especially if you come from a Bash or configuration-management background.
Here is the beginner mental model:

That model is not wrong, but it hides some operational problems. Provisioners can fail halfway through. They can depend on SSH availability. They can make repeated applies unpredictable. They can blur the separation between “Terraform manages infrastructure state” and “something else manages software configuration.”
So before you treat provisioners as the default answer, learn their mechanics and their tradeoffs.

sections.title: The Three Common Provisioners
paragraphs: Terraform's most common provisioners are:
Each one does something slightly different.

sections.title: local-exec: Run Commands on the Machine Running Terraform
paragraphs: local-exec executes a command on the local machine where Terraform is running. That might be:
After Terraform creates the EC2 instance, it runs the local shell command and appends the instance public IP to inventory.txt on the machine running Terraform.
local-exec does not run on the created resource. It runs locally. That distinction matters a lot.
If Terraform runs inside GitLab CI, the command runs in the CI job container or runner environment, not on your EC2 instance.

sections.title: remote-exec: Run Commands on the Provisioned Resource
paragraphs: remote-exec runs commands on the target machine itself, usually over SSH for Linux hosts or WinRM for Windows.
This is one of the most common provisioner examples you will see.
It lets Terraform create the VM and then configure software on it immediately. That can make a tutorial seem smooth because one terraform apply produces a working server.
This setup assumes all of the following are true at the exact right time:
If any one of those assumptions breaks, the apply fails even though the infrastructure resource itself may already exist.

sections.title: file: Copy Files to a Remote Resource
paragraphs: The file provisioner copies a file or directory from the Terraform runner to the remote resource.
You often see file combined with remote-exec:
Again, it works, but it turns Terraform into a machine bootstrap-and-configure tool, which is not its strongest role.

sections.title: The connection Block
paragraphs: Both remote-exec and file usually need a connection block. This tells Terraform how to reach the remote host.
Other useful fields can include:
Inside a provisioner or connection block, self refers to the resource being provisioned. So self.public_ip means “use the public IP of this resource.”
That is convenient, but it also shows how tightly provisioners depend on resource timing and runtime connectivity.

sections.title: Provisioners Run on Create or Destroy
paragraphs: Provisioners normally run when a resource is created. Some can also run at destroy time.
Example destroy provisioner:
Destroy-time provisioners are even trickier than create-time ones because they fire during teardown, when resources may already be disappearing.
If the destroy-time cleanup is truly critical, you should think carefully about whether Terraform is the right place to model it.

sections.title: Why HashiCorp Recommends Against Provisioners
paragraphs: This is the most important section of the lesson.
HashiCorp recommends avoiding provisioners where possible because they are often:

Provisioners depend on live connectivity, timing, credentials, and runtime behavior. Infrastructure might be created successfully while the provisioner still fails. That leaves you with partial success and messy recovery.
Terraform is strongest when you describe the desired end state. Provisioners push you back toward procedural steps: run this command, then this file copy, then restart that service.

Idempotence means you can run the same operation repeatedly and converge on the same result. Provisioners often make that harder, especially if scripts append, mutate, or depend on current machine state.
Terraform is an infrastructure provisioning tool. Configuration management tools such as Ansible are built specifically for software installation, service management, and repeated host configuration.
Terraform can show you the plan for resource changes. It cannot give you a rich preview of the side effects inside your shell commands. That reduces predictability.

sections.title: Better Alternatives to Provisioners
paragraphs: HashiCorp does not say “never automate post-provision tasks.” It says “use better-native patterns first.”
For VM bootstrapping, user_data and cloud-init are usually cleaner than remote-exec.
If the same packages and files should exist on every VM, bake them into a machine image with Packer instead of installing them during every Terraform apply.
If you need rich configuration management, Ansible is usually a better tool than Terraform provisioners. It is built for:
If the post-provision step is “deploy the app,” that step often belongs in CI/CD, not inside Terraform.

sections.title: When Provisioners Are Acceptable

If yes, choose that instead.
If no, a small carefully scoped provisioner may be acceptable.

A null_resource does not create real infrastructure. It is just a Terraform-managed placeholder that can run provisioners.
triggers is a map of values Terraform watches. If one of those values changes, Terraform replaces the null_resource, which causes the provisioner to run again.

But it also makes it easy to abuse Terraform as a generic task runner.
This can be handy, but again, ask whether the task belongs in Terraform at all.

sections.title: Frequently Asked Questions
paragraphs: What are Terraform provisioners and should I use them?

Provisioners run scripts or commands as part of resource creation or destruction, local-exec on the machine running Terraform, remote-exec over SSH or WinRM on the created resource. HashiCorp explicitly describes them as a last resort, and that guidance is sound: they break Terraform's declarative model, are not represented in state, and cannot be planned. Use them only when no provider, cloud-init or configuration management alternative exists.
Why are provisioners considered a last resort?

Because Terraform cannot reason about them. A provisioner's effects are invisible to the plan, are not recorded in state, and are not re-run when the underlying script changes, so the resource can be "up to date" while the configuration it applied is stale. They also introduce a network and credential dependency at apply time, which makes applies fail for reasons unrelated to infrastructure. Failures mark the resource tainted, forcing a destroy and recreate on the next run.
What should I use instead of a provisioner?

For bootstrapping a machine, use user_data or cloud-init, which the cloud provider executes and which is part of the resource's own configuration. For configuring software, use Ansible, Chef or Puppet after Terraform has created the infrastructure. For baking software into an image, use Packer so instances start ready. For calling an API a provider does not cover, prefer a dedicated provider or an external data source over local-exec and curl.
What does it mean when a resource is tainted?

A provisioner failed, so Terraform marks the resource as unreliable. The infrastructure exists but its configuration did not complete. The next plan proposes destroying and recreating it, because Terraform has no way to re-run just the provisioner. You can clear the mark with terraform untaint if you fixed the problem by hand, though that leaves Terraform trusting a state it did not create.
How do destroy-time provisioners work?

Adding when = destroy runs the provisioner before the resource is destroyed, typically to deregister a node or drain connections. They come with real constraints: they cannot reference variables or most other values, only self, and they must still be present in configuration when the destroy happens, so removing the resource block and the provisioner together means the provisioner never runs. Plan the removal in two steps if a destroy-time action matters.
Is local-exec ever acceptable?

For genuinely local, idempotent side effects that do not represent infrastructure. Writing a kubeconfig for a subsequent step, or triggering a notification. It is pragmatic and widely used. It becomes a problem when it is doing work that should be declarative, because nothing plans it, nothing detects drift in it, and nobody reviewing the plan can see what it will do. If a local-exec is creating or modifying infrastructure, that infrastructure belongs in a resource block.

sections.title: Why Infrastructure as Code Belongs in CI/CD
paragraphs: Terraform gives you reproducible infrastructure, but if engineers still apply changes manually from their laptops, you only solved half the problem.
A CI/CD pipeline turns Terraform from “code that could be run consistently” into “code that is run consistently.” That matters for several reasons.
The same validation and deployment steps run every time. You do not rely on one engineer remembering the right command sequence.
Pipelines attach infrastructure actions to commits, branches, merge requests, and job logs. That makes it far easier to answer questions like:

“Cowboy infrastructure” means someone changes production directly from a laptop, outside a reviewable pipeline, often with local credentials and local state. CI/CD reduces that risk by making the pipeline the normal path.
A good pipeline can validate automatically, publish a plan artifact, and require a manual approval before apply. That creates a safer change-management flow without slowing teams down too much.
Once more than one person manages infrastructure, a pipeline becomes the easiest way to standardize execution.

sections.title: The Standard Terraform Pipeline Pattern
paragraphs: A practical GitLab Terraform pipeline often follows this flow:
Each phase has a specific purpose:
This separation matters. You do not want “validate and deploy immediately” as your only option.

codeBlock.code: validate  ->  plan  ->  apply (manual)  ->  destroy (manual)

sections.title: The Full GitLab CI/CD Example
paragraphs: Below is a complete .gitlab-ci.yml example for a Terraform project that uses GitLab-managed Terraform state and AWS credentials supplied through CI/CD variables.
This pipeline is intentionally simple and production-minded. It validates on branches and merge requests, always produces a plan, and only allows apply or destroy manually on the default branch.

codeBlock.code:
image: hashicorp/terraform:1.9.8

stages:
  - validate
  - plan
  - apply
  - destroy

variables:
  TF_ROOT: .
  TF_IN_AUTOMATION: "true"
  TF_INPUT: "false"
  TF_STATE_NAME: "aws-project"
  TF_PLAN_FILE: "tfplan"
  TF_CLI_ARGS_init: "-no-color"
  TF_CLI_ARGS_plan: "-no-color"
  TF_CLI_ARGS_apply: "-no-color"
  TF_CLI_ARGS_destroy: "-no-color"

before_script:
  - cd "$TF_ROOT"
  - terraform version

sections.title: Frequently Asked Questions
paragraphs: How should a Terraform CI/CD pipeline be structured?

Run fmt -check, validate and a security scan on every commit. On pull requests, run terraform plan -out=tfplan and post the output as a comment so the change is reviewable. On merge to the default branch, apply the saved plan file rather than re-planning, so what was approved is exactly what runs. Gate production behind a manual approval, and never let apply run from a feature branch against shared infrastructure.
Why should CI apply a saved plan file?

Because without it, the apply recalculates from whatever state and real infrastructure exist at that moment, which may differ from what the reviewer saw. terraform plan -out=tfplan followed by terraform apply tfplan guarantees the approved change is the applied change. The caveat is that a plan file contains sensitive values in plain text, so treat the artifact as a secret and expire it quickly.
How do I authenticate Terraform to AWS from CI without access keys?

Use OIDC. Register your CI provider as an OIDC identity provider in AWS, create a role whose trust policy accepts its tokens with conditions restricting the specific repository and branch, and have the pipeline exchange a short-lived token for temporary credentials. Nothing long-lived is stored, there is nothing to rotate, and a leaked log contains no reusable secret. The equivalent mechanism exists for Azure and GCP.
How do I stop two pipeline runs applying at once?

State locking, which a proper remote backend provides. S3 with native locking or a DynamoDB table, or Terraform Cloud. The second run then waits or fails rather than corrupting state. Add pipeline-level concurrency control as well, since queueing at the CI layer produces a clearer outcome than a lock timeout. If a run is killed mid-apply the lock can stick, and terraform force-unlock clears it once you have confirmed nothing is actually running.
Should terraform apply be fully automatic?

For non-production, yes. Fast feedback is worth more than the risk. For production, a manual approval gate is the norm, because a plan can contain a resource replacement that destroys data and no amount of automated checking reliably catches intent. A reasonable middle ground is automatic apply when the plan contains only additions and in-place updates, with approval required whenever it contains a destroy or a replacement.
How do I handle multiple environments in one pipeline?

Keep a separate state file per environment and run the same pipeline with different backend configuration and credentials, supplied via -backend-config and -var-file. Promote by applying identical code to each environment in turn, dev, then staging, then production, rather than maintaining divergent branches. Scope each environment's credentials to that environment alone, so a pipeline misconfiguration cannot reach production from a staging job.

commonPitfalls: Deploying changes to production without dry-running or checking execution plans.
Neglecting automated healthchecks, probe timeouts, and resource quota boundaries.
Failing to pin immutable versions or image digests in production manifests.

sections.title: Why Terraform Security Scanning Matters
paragraphs: Terraform makes infrastructure repeatable, but repeatable does not automatically mean secure.

If you write an insecure S3 bucket policy, a security group that opens SSH to the world, or an unencrypted EBS volume, Terraform will happily create it consistently every time. That is why Infrastructure as Code security matters so much.
Misconfigured cloud infrastructure is one of the most common causes of cloud incidents. In many breaches, the root problem is not a sophisticated zero-day. It is something simpler:

sections.title: Frequently Asked Questions
paragraphs: What is the difference between tfsec and Checkov?

Both scan Terraform for insecure configuration before it is applied. tfsec is Terraform-specific, fast, and has since been folded into Trivy, which is where new development happens. Checkov covers Terraform alongside CloudFormation, Kubernetes manifests, Helm charts and Dockerfiles, has a larger policy set, and supports custom policies in Python as well as YAML. Running both catches slightly different things; if you run one, Checkov's breadth usually wins for a mixed estate.
Where in the pipeline should security scanning run?

On every pull request, before the plan is approved, that is the whole point of shifting left, since a misconfiguration caught in review costs minutes and the same one caught in production costs an incident. Scanning is fast enough to run on every commit. Add a second scan of the deployed state periodically, because policies change and a configuration that passed six months ago may not pass today.
Should a security finding fail the build?

Fail on high and critical severity in changed code; report the rest without blocking. A policy of zero findings across an existing codebase gets disabled within a month, because the backlog blocks unrelated work and people route around it. Gating on newly introduced high-severity issues keeps the signal meaningful while the existing backlog is worked through separately.
How do I suppress a false positive properly?

Use an inline annotation, #tfsec:ignore:aws-s3-enable-versioning or #checkov:skip=CKV_AWS_21:Bucket is ephemeral build cache, placed on the specific resource, with a reason. Two rules make this safe: never suppress globally when a resource-level suppression will do, and always include the justification, because an unexplained skip is indistinguishable from someone silencing a real finding. Review suppressions periodically; they accumulate.
What are the most common security problems these tools find?

Publicly accessible S3 buckets, security groups allowing 0.0.0.0/0 on SSH or database ports, unencrypted EBS volumes and RDS instances, IAM policies granting wildcard actions or resources, missing access logging, and unencrypted data in transit. Most are one line to fix and are far cheaper to catch in a pull request than in a penetration test or a breach.
Does scanning replace reviewing the plan?

No. Static analysis catches known misconfiguration patterns; it cannot tell you that a change will replace your production database, delete a bucket that holds data, or apply to the wrong account. Those come from reading the plan. Particularly the -/+ replacement markers. Scanning and plan review answer different questions and both belong in the pipeline.
